utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. Madam Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14-A, the Prosecutor versus Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. May I now call for appearances. For the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Norman Farrell, Mr. Mark Harmon, Ms. Sonja Boelaert-Suominen, Ms. Kelly Howick, and our case manager today is Nicky Bonfield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. For the appellant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For the appellant, Russell Hayman, joined by my co-counsel Anto Nobilo, and to my furthest left, Andrew Paley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we can start our hearing. I will make some preliminary remarks about today's hearing which has been called by the Appeals Chamber pursuant to the Scheduling Order issued on 31 October 2002. In the Scheduling Order, as you know, the Appeals Chamber addressed all of these three Rule 115 motions that had been filed by the appellant as of that date. The Appeals Chamber found that a substantial number of exhibits submitted with the first and second motion and two statements submitted with the third motion were clearly admissible on appeal. As to the other items of additional evidence sought to be admitted by the appellant in the motions, the Appeals Chamber has reserved its position at this time. The Appeals Chamber further considered that in light of the sheer volume of additional evidence identified as clearly admissible, the possible submission of rebuttal evidence and the potential of additional evidence to bring about a redetermination of the facts of the case, it would be more appropriate for any redetermination of the facts to be made by a Trial Chamber. On this issue, the Appeals Chamber has decided to hear the views of the parties. Therefore, the subject of this hearing is limited by the terms of the Scheduling Order to the issue of whether the clearly admissible evidence identified in that order justifies a new trial by a Trial Chamber on some or all the counts. In the Scheduling Order, the parties have also been directed to refrain from discussing the admissibility of the additional evidence submitted thus far in relation to which the Appeals Chamber has reserved its position at this time. This is not a hearing to entertain arguments on the admissibility of that additional evidence under Rule 115. It is a hearing to provide the parties with the opportunity to submit before the Appeals Chamber their views on whether a new trial is warranted in this case in order to assist the Chamber on this issue. In order to facilitate the discussion, the parties have also been directed, pursuant to the Scheduling Order, to file a book of authorities on which they intend to rely at the hearing. We have received such books of authorities and thank the parties for their submission. Now, as it is a general principle pursuant to the Statute and the Rules of this Tribunal, the hearing today will be held in open session generally. Should it become necessary to go into closed session for reasons of dealing with documents submitted under seal, we will do so. I will only ask counsel to raise that request at the appropriate stage when they would wish that to happen and we will rule on that. A second Scheduling Order on today's hearing was issued on 14 November 2002. We are familiar with the content of this order. I simply remind you that the Prosecution will have 75 minutes to present its oral argument. After a break, counsel for the appellant will then have in turn 75 minutes to present their arguments. We will have then another break, and we will reconvene to hear the reply of the Prosecution, who will have 30 minutes, and of the appellant who will have another 30 minutes. As usual, at the end of each presentation, members of the Bench may ask questions if they so wish. I ask everybody to keep this schedule in mind. Now, if all this is clear, if there are no problems, we will go on to hear the first presentation. The Prosecution has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Pocar, Your Honours, if I may. According to the Scheduling Order on October 31st, the issue to be argued today before you is whether or not the admitted documents, the 47 documents and the two witness statements, justifies a new trial. With respect, it appears that there's an assumption in this order that you have the authority to do so at this stage and that the question you're asking the parties to brief is whether, in fact, it's justified. I will start my submissions with the argument that, in fact, under the law of this Tribunal as it presently stands, both the law as established in Kupreskic and the law as reflected presently in Rule 115, this Court does not have the authority at this stage to order a new trial. After making those submissions, I will then turn to the issues related to if the Court does or intends to proceed to that determination after this hearing, whether or not it is justified to order a new trial at this stage, and what the practical considerations and arguments are which the Prosecution relies on to say that it's not. First of all, the first issue is whether or not the Appeals Chamber actually has the authority at this stage to order a new trial. There are five points which I will make throughout my submissions, but I will summarise them now. The first is that the procedural law, as established by this very Chamber in the last case that dealt with this matter, Kupreskic, determined that this was not the stage at which a new trial could be ordered. Secondly, Rule 115, as presently amended, establishes a procedure before this Court that it can reach its final determination under Rule 117. It does not envisage the possibility of a new trial at the admissibility stage. Thirdly, the standard for ordering a new trial under Article 25 is not the standard for admissibility and, therefore, if it is simply the admissibility that has been decided at this point, there is no basis upon which you can then reconcile that with the standard that there must be an error of fact which warrants a new trial. Fourthly, the possibility of ordering a retrial after the admissibility standard has been met is not the practice of this Tribunal or of the Rwanda Tribunal, the Appeals Chamber of the Rwanda Tribunal, and I'll refer to two cases there where this was not followed. And lastly, in the Prosecution's submission, this possibility has not been the basis upon which this appeal has proceeded. The Prosecution proceeded in this case on the basis that though it had evidence to show that a new trial was not warranted, it would not present it at the admissibility stage. That's specifically reflected in paragraphs 9 to 11 of the Prosecution's response to the second 115 motion. And, as I will respectfully submit, is clear from the arguments that were made and the decision that was -- which resulted from the Kupreskic case. The approach that was followed in this appeal was the one required and mandated by the Kupreskic Appeals Chamber and the Prosecution never received any indication to the contrary. Thirdly, the Prosecution proceeded based on Kupreskic on the basis that the evidence would be tested before an ultimate determination would be made. And lastly, the Prosecution proceeded on the basis of the decision of the Appeals Chamber on the 24th of September that further submissions would be filed after the additional evidence was admitted. In my respectful submission, it appears that the Appeals Chamber proceeded on the same basis as the Prosecution did, and on the same basis as established under the procedural law in Kupreskic until the recent scheduling order. The appropriate way to proceed in this case is that the Appeals Chamber should remain seised of this matter and should deal with the additional evidence. If this Chamber deems it completely necessary, Kupreskic instructed that it can remit the matter to a Trial Chamber for the issues related to additional evidence, not for a new trial. And then the Appeals Chamber can consider that additional evidence and any findings by the Tribunal of fact in its ultimate determination, based on the test expressed in Kupreskic as to what the Appeals Chamber must find to overturn the verdict. This procedure, it is respectfully submitted, has been adopted by the ICTR in the Musema case and in the Kambanda case. As I'm sure this Chamber's fully aware, in the Musema case, the Appeals Chamber specifically refers to the procedure and the standards set out in Kupreskic. It heard evidence before it, and it proceeded to make a determination. I will proceed on the basis of those legal submissions on whether you have the authority to order a new trial. I will return to the issue of if you do, whether it justifies it in the circumstances of this case. Let me just make one final comment before I take you to the Kupreskic judgement, and I'll make two references to the Kupreskic Appeals Chamber's judgement. If you have it with you, I'll tell you where I'm referring to. But essentially, the Kupreskic Appeals Chamber and the rules require a two-stage process. With respect, this Appeals Chamber is considering conflating that process. The Appeals Chamber is vested with the specific authority under Rule 115 to hear additional evidence. It's respectfully submitted that the Chamber cannot be vested with the authority to be a trier of fact but then decline to exercise that function. The threshold for admissibility is very low, and this is one of the submissions that the Prosecution will be relying on as to whether or not it meets the standard for a new trial, when in fact all that's been determined now is that the material is admissible. It's submitted that Kupreskic requires that you must test the evidence, that's the Appeals Chamber or Trial Chamber designate for that particular issue. At paragraph 70, of the Kupreskic decision, which I'll refer to, paragraph 70 specifically deals with the issue of testing the admitted evidence. What that Chamber has held is that -- and now I quote, "Where the Rule 115 evidence is accepted for consideration, the Appeals Chamber has, in effect, decided that the evidence is sufficiently important, that if it had been before the Trial Chamber, the conclusion of guilt could have been different." At that stage of the proceedings, the new evidence may not have been subjected to any form of adversarial scrutiny, as the case here , save for the Appeals Chamber's initial assessment as to whether it was, on its face, credible. It may be that there's no dispute between the parties as to this issue, but it is more likely that the opposing party challenges the veracity of the additional evidence. The Appeals Chamber is faced with a choice. Either it can test the evidence itself to determine veracity or order the case to be remitted to a Trial Chamber to hear the new evidence. There is no third choice that the Trial Chamber -- the Appeals Chamber can decide at that stage without any testing that there is an error of fact under Article 25 warranting a new trial. And more so, it does not say that where the evidence to be tested is extensive or there's an extensive volume of it that you can lower the standard and apply the admissibility standard for a determination of whether a new trial is warranted. The new language of Rule 115 expressly recognises this. The Rule recognises that rebuttal material may be presented by an affected party. Further, the more recent amendments of Rule 115, in my submission, reflect the exact passages that I will refer to in Kupreskic. Rule 115 (B) says: "The Appeals Chamber will consider the additional evidence and any rebuttal along with that already on the record to arrive at a final judgement in accordance with Rule 117." It submits that if you can't reach a final judgement, to order a new trial on the basis of Rule 115 prior to that procedure being instituted. The standard under Rule 115 is a different standard than that to be applied to overturn a verdict. If the standard was the same, then it would be one process. It's not the same. The Kupreskic Appeals Chamber specifically states it's not the same and specifically declines to adopt the one-stage process. How can this Appeals Chamber conclude that there was objectively an incorrectness of fact as required by Tadic and by Kupreskic based on untested evidence and where there's been in submissions? How does the standard for admissibility, which could have had an impact on the verdict, reach the level required in Kupreskic to overturn the verdict? Even more troubling is how can the Appeals Chamber order a new trial on evidence which "appears to be capable of belief"? The evidence before you hasn't been found to be capable of belief. It's only been found to appear to be capable of belief according to the standard adopted. With respect, the trial, which took 25 months, 170 witnesses, and thousands of pages of exhibits should not be overturned simply on documents which appear to be capable of belief. The answer to these questions is clearly the Appeals Chamber does not have the authority under Kupreskic or Rule 115.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you. The cases and propositions which are before you, the cases which are in the books of authorities, I ask you to take note of the cases and look at the cases that were before the Kupreskic Appeals Chamber judgement. You'll find that they are almost exactly the same. I can also inform you and submit that these issues were completely argued in Kupreskic. The Defence counsel in Kupreskic argued that this standard that was proposed and adopted is too high a standard and that the Appeals Chamber should adopt a could standard, if the evidence could. These cases and those submissions were before the Appeals Chamber, and we argued it extensively, and, quite frankly, it was rejected. The Appeals Chamber may come to a different standard, but if the Appeals Chamber is applying what is essentially a could standard, an admissibility standard, it's already been rejected. That was the submission of the Defence in Kupreskic. Mr. Clegg, specifically for the appellant Josipovic, argued this issue. And you can see from the Appeals Chamber that they referred extensively to those cases, and they did not accept that at the admissibility stage the matter would be sent back for a new trial or that the standard would be that it could affect the verdict, which warrants a new trial. The issue of testing was also subject to much litigation, I can attest to, in the Kupreskic case. Now, the Court may say that it's going to adopt a standard that if it's reasonably capable of belief, it should go back for a new trial. That standard, quite frankly, was not accepted for overturning the verdict but is only the standard for admissibility. But even assuming that you're going to accept the standard that the admissibility is sufficient to warrant a new trial, you would still have to test the evidence. You simply couldn't decide that it's reasonably capable of belief without testing it. No Court would do that, in my respectful submission. In fact, this was the issue we litigated in Kupreskic. If I could turn you to page 63 of the Appeals Chamber's decision in Kupreskic. As you'll see from the passage I intend to read from, which is paragraph 63, you'll see that what took place was that the Prosecution indicated that it had material which it intended to file which went to the ultimate issue as to whether or not you would order a new trial. Some of it went to credibility, and some of it went to the impact of the verdict -- sorry, the impact of the evidence on the verdict. The Appeals Chamber specifically stated, "This is not the stage to do it. You do it after, and we'll hear it. And we may even decide after we hear your submissions and hear the evidence that our initial impression was wrong." And what they say in paragraph 63 is that: "The credibility component is linked to the danger that appellate proceedings can be abused by a party presenting evidence to the appeal body that appears to be relevant to a material issue, but that has not been tested in the crucible of a trial. In this case, however, the Appeals Chamber was also concerned that at the relatively early stage of the appeal, that the motions for additional evidence were received, the main proceedings should not be unduly delayed by protracted proceedings litigating credibility of evidence tendered in the Rule 115 motions. It would have been counter-productive for the Appeals Chamber to require the parties to present copious amounts of supplementary evidence to demonstrate the veracity of the new evidence, taking up time and resources of the court as well as the parties, only to rule later that the additional evidence did not have the potential of demonstrating that a conviction or sentence was unsafe. The most appropriate course, it was felt at the time, was to apply a relatively low threshold for credit in admitting additional evidence." Then it states that the test is: "...does the evidence appear to be reasonably capable of belief or reliance?" The practice of this Chamber is that any evidence that the Prosecution has which goes to testing the veracity of the documents, testing the impact, and demonstrating that a new trial would be warranted takes place at the second stage. It's respectfully submitted that by considering at this stage to order a new trial, you are not only depriving yourself of the benefit of documents or evidence which would demonstrate that no new trial is warranted, but you're actually proceeding on a basis which was not envisaged by Kupreskic and was envisaged by the practice of the Prosecution as a result of this ruling. The ruling in Kupreskic makes good sense. As a logical matter, this Chamber would not want to hear evidence with respect to credibility or impact for the ultimate determination at the threshold stage in case the Court decides that it wasn't admissible. In the Kupreskic case, there was 25 motions for additional evidence. There was 114 items put forward. There was 36 witnesses. There was statements of witnesses that lasted four days. There was testimony from trials. The Court -- the Prosecution indicated its intention to challenge the veracity of some of this evidence and its impact, and the Court said, "No. You'll get the opportunity to determine that on the stage as to whether or not you should -- we should order a new trial." It's also interesting that the importance of testing the evidence was in essence conceded by the appellant in this very case. When the appellant submitted the three new witness statements, the Prosecution objected on the basis that they were inadmissible. They were in no form that would be admissible before this Chamber or before any Chamber before this Tribunal, excepting that Rule 92 bis applies on appeal, which the Kupreskic Appeals Chamber found that it did, the material wouldn't be admissible here or at a trial level. The Defence counsel in their response said, "We're not tendering it as evidence. We're tendering it as prima facie evidence to show the Court that it would be admissible." In my submission, clearly acknowledging there is a second stage before the Court can rely on it. What the result is, then, is that the parties are proceeding and the Prosecution is proceeding on the basis to admit it. The Defence acknowledged that it's actually not evidence before you, but it's only prima facie evidence for admissibility, and they invite the Appeals Chamber to actually have the witnesses come and permit the Prosecution to cross-examine them. And now by the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: My apologies. Now by the procedure which is envisioned here, that very issue will not be granted. Before turning to the second stage of my submission, I simply note that there are a number of domestic jurisdictions which are presented to the Chamber by both parties. As indicated, these decisions have already been considered and the standard by the Appeals Chamber has been established in Kupreskic. If the standard which has been submitted and which is found in these cases which permit an Appeals Chamber to consider ordering a new trial at the admissibility stage, most of these cases and certainly the persuasive ones say that the evidence must be tested. Even if you accept a standard from national jurisdictions that once it's shown that the evidence could affect a verdict, you would order a new trial, and you've heard the Prosecution's submissions on that. It's not the law of this Tribunal and it was already debated, but even if you do, the cases say that it won't be sent back on that standard until it's tested. So not only is it not tested in this case, it's not following, as I've indicated, the standard in Kupreskic. If you look at the main case cited, Clegg, Luvaglio, or the Canadian cases: Levesque; Stolar, it's a Canadian case; or the "Salhany" procedural law textbook in Canada, they indicate that the -- before a determination can be made, the evidence must be tested. Now I'll turn to the second argument of the Prosecution which is that if you do have the authority under the law of the Tribunal to order a new trial at this stage, I submit that the new evidence does not justify a new trial at this stage. There are five points which I will make in my submissions, and I'll just outline them now. And these are five issues which, in the Prosecution's submission, I think that the Scheduling Order essentially indicates should be addressed. The first is whether, on the basis of the evidence presented before it at this stage, a new trial is justified. And I take that as being "at this stage" being at the stage where there has been no testing. That's the procedure we're at now. The second question is whether the sheer volume of the 47 documents and the two witnesses warrants a new trial. The third issue alluded to in the judgement is whether the complexity of the case at this stage warrants a new trial. The fourth issue is whether or not it is better that a Trial Chamber hear this evidence and not the Appeals Chamber. And the fifth, which seems to be implied, though it's not explicit, is whether there is a requirement for a rehearing of the entire case. Starting with the first issue concerning the justification of a new trial on the evidence as you have it before you. I would like to take you through some documents in relation to the ones admitted, and I will be referring to the material which was provided to the Court, that's the documents to be referred to by the Prosecution at the oral hearing. If I can start by taking you to -- you'll see in the front, it's an attempt to have an index. It doesn't have the registry page numbers - I'm sorry we didn't have them at the time we created it - but if I can start by -- I'm not going to go through all of these, they are just illustrative to support the Prosecution's argument. If I may start with Exhibit 146, which has been admitted, it's registry page number 16.796 in the material before you, if you follow the page numbers at the bottom, Your Honours, it's -- page 107 is the first English one. Exhibit 146 that's been filed by the appellant to demonstrate that the appellant Blaskic is reminding his commanders to comply with international humanitarian law. This is on April 24th, 1993, and it's in relation to the zone of responsibility of Kiseljak. Now, the name at the bottom, Bozic, is Blaskic's direct subordinate in the operative zone. Now, if you look at the document, you'll see that in the first paragraph, it indicates that the following order by Brigadier Commander Bozic is pursuant to two orders. The second one I'd ask you to take note of, order number 01-4-546/93 of April 24th, 1993; that's Blaskic's order. And this material is put forward to show that Blaskic actually informed his commanders in Kiseljak to comply with international humanitarian law. And the significance of this document is, in fact, that it's Blaskic's orders that they're relying on. And this was admitted as a new document not available at trial, and this was admitted under the basis that it was from the Zagreb archives and not admissible. If you turn over two pages to page 109 at the bottom, you'll see an order from Blaskic requiring three things, and if you look at the top left-hand side, the order number is 01-4-546/93. This is the order that's referred to in the Bozic order. The Bozic order is put in for the purpose of showing that General Blaskic is giving orders to his subordinates. One would presume that this order is actually the more exculpatory because it actually demonstrates that an order was given, and this is the order and this is the content of the order. Therefore, this is actually more exculpatory or more important than the order to Bozic. This was Exhibit -- Defence Exhibit 362 at trial, and the Prosecution's submission is it's hard to imagine how an exhibit which has been admitted for the purpose of demonstrating that Blaskic issued orders is somehow going to warrant a new trial when the actual order it's relying on was submitted by the Defence already. If I can ask you to turn over a few pages to page 112 in the right-hand corner, it's registry page 16.791. This is Defence Exhibit 147 admitted on this appeal. Once again, it's presented by the appellant as being a document which shows that Blaskic issued an order which they complied with. If you look in the first paragraph of this order, it says that the order was issued pursuant to order number 01-4-560/93 of the 24th of April, 1993. Once again, this is submitted to show that the order of Blaskic was specifically to comply with international humanitarian law. The inference, once again, is that if it shows that there was an order, the inference being that there is an order directly from General Blaskic to comply with international humanitarian law in relation to the Kiseljak region. If I could ask you to turn over two pages, please, to page 114 in the bottom right-hand corner, you'll see that this is the order and if you turn over to the next page, you'll see the French version which specifically has the reference number 01-4-560/93. Now, presumably, this order itself is the more exculpatory of the two, because it actually is issued by General Blaskic. It actually shows that he issued an order to the Kiseljak region on April 24th, 1993, asking them to comply with international humanitarian law; therefore it's, of course, presumably of more weight than the order of the subordinate which just refers to his order. This was Exhibit D-78 at trial. Once again, the Prosecution fails to see how these documents are such that the Appeals Chamber on the basis of documents that were essentially before the Trial Chamber, actually better documents before the Trial Chamber, would be such that you would consider these in warranting a new trial. And lastly on these two documents, I'd note one final thing: The Defence of Blaskic at trial was that he was cut off from Kiseljak, and that therefore he had no communication or control in Kiseljak. He puts in these orders from Bozic to demonstrate that he actually issued proper orders. Well, that was clearly before the Trial Chamber, in fact, better orders were before the Trial Chamber and it made no difference. So what we have then is we have documents of no exculpatory value in relation to the Trial Chamber's finding, but documents which show that there was orders received by the Kiseljak Operative Command on two days in the middle of April during the fighting and, in fact, these documents are inculpatory. They refute the Defence argument that he had no ability to communicate with Kiseljak because it was shut off. If I may now refer you to Exhibit 14. This is the Defence Exhibit 14 which was admitted on the appeal. It's page 51 of the documents to be referred to by the Prosecution. It's registry page 16.852. You'll note that this is a report in March of 1994. It's approximately almost one year after the event in Ahmici. It's an intelligence report which is unsourced and which has no evidence to substantiate it. It's just assertions made in an intelligence report in Zagreb from the son of Franjo Tudjman to Franjo Tudjman, the President of Zagreb. There's a number of references in here, and I can address them if you wish, but I'd just like to refer to one reference in this document. On the next page of the document, you'll see there's full text the length of the page, and in the beginning of the second full text -- I'm sorry, second full paragraph in the text there's reference to Mario Cerkez. Now, the Defence theory is that Blaskic cannot be responsible for Ahmici for a number of reasons, one being that the Vitez Brigade was not in Ahmici. The Vitez Brigade falls under Mario Cerkez and reports directly to General Blaskic. This is one of his regular units which was never disputed during the trial, and Blaskic indicated that they were a regular unit falling under his command. The appellant was convicted at trial on the basis that the Vitez Brigade was in Ahmici. His additional evidence here - and there's one reliance on the war diary - is this comment and this is the only comment in relation to Mario Cerkez before you, is the comment that Mario Cerkez -- I apologise, was not involved in the massacre in Ahmici. That's the new evidence in relation to the Vitez Brigade in Ahmici in March 1994. If I can just take you to the material which follows, if you turn to two pages over which is page 55 at the bottom, you'll see a report dated the 16th of April at 10.00 to Blaskic. At the top, you'll see to the command of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, that's General Blaskic. And you'll see at the bottom that it's from the Brigade Commander Mario Cerkez. It's at 10.00 in the morning on the 16th of April, the day that the attack on Ahmici started. The title of the report is Report on the Situation in the Area of Responsibility. If you look at about the middle of the page with the words beginning, "Our forces are advancing." You'll see that it says, "Our forces are advancing on Donja Veceriska, whose fall is imminent, and in Ahmici." This is at 10.00 in the morning of the attack in Ahmici, an order from Mario Cerkez of the Vitez Brigade to General Blaskic. If I can ask you to turn over two more pages to page reference 57 at the bottom right-hand corner. This is an order dated April 16th at 10.35; it's 35 minutes after the previous order. It's an order from Blaskic to the commander of the Vitez Brigade, that's Mario Cerkez. It says, "The following shall be done in connection with your report number," then it lists the number. That's the previous order I just showed you. It says, "Capture the villages of Donja Veceriska, Ahmici, Sivrino Selo, and Vrhovine completely." At 10.35 in the morning, General Blaskic, who claims he doesn't know anything about Ahmici, who claims he didn't even find out about it about the crimes until the 22nd, and who claims that he was the commander of the Vitez Brigade, but the Vitez Brigade was not present, was giving an order to the Vitez Brigade to basically completely capture Ahmici at 10.30 in the morning. If I can ask you to turn over three pages to page 60 at the bottom right-hand side. This is, as you can see in the top left-hand corner, a report on April 16, 1993. There's no time, but based on the previous order and the following order, I will show you that this has to be between 10.00 a.m. and 2.00 in the afternoon on April 16th. This is from the Vitez Brigade to Blaskic. Under number 1 it says, second paragraph under number 1: "The village of Ahmici is also 70 per cent done..." Once again, this is conclusive evidence that General Blaskic had the Vitez Brigade involved in the attack on Ahmici. And I'll note you'll see in the judgement, if you go back to it, that the position of General Blaskic was that the Vitez Brigade was not involved in the fighting. That was his defence. I think the orders speak for themselves. Lastly, I'd ask you to turn to the document, page 62 at the bottom. This is an order from General Blaskic to Mario Cerkez, Commander of the Vitez Brigade, referring to the previous order or the previous report which I just took you to, and it says under paragraph 2: "Continue the activities described under item 1 of your report." If you go back, item 1 includes the attack on Ahmici being 70 per cent done. I won't continue with the documents that are listed behind Exhibit 14. What the Prosecution's submission is is that if permitted to file material on this issue, based on the one document which you've admitted, which is an unsubstantiated intelligence report in Zagreb that Mario Cerkez wasn't involved, a report that was written in March of 1994 - of course if the Chamber had the benefit of the material which the Prosecution would file - based on this evidence before you now and an unsubstantiated intelligence report almost a year later. I think there is no doubt that the Appeals Chamber would not think it sufficient to order a new trial on Ahmici to the extent that he's liable for the involvement of the Vitez Brigade. If I can take you lastly to Exhibit 88. This is page 74 of the documents to be referred to. This relates to the special unit called the Vitezovi. The Vitezovi was considered to be a special unit that was within the command structure of General Blaskic and assisted in the fighting in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. The position of the appellant in his first additional evidence motion is that the Vitezovi were commanded from Mostar. Therefore, it was a parallel chain of command and outside his chain of command, and that in addition to be commanded from Mostar, which is a de jure argument, the position also in their first additional evidence motion is that he actually had no de facto control over the Vitezovi and that even though he was surrounded in a pocket with the Vitezovi within his command formation, they actually didn't take any orders from him. That was rejected by the Appeals Chamber -- by the Trial Chamber, I'm sorry. This document is one of a number of documents - I think there's six - that are filed to demonstrate that the Vitezovi were outside of the control of General Blaskic. I don't need to list the others ones, but they've been admitted as part of the 47 documents. I take this one, this exact document, because of the time of it. This is on the 17th of April, 1993. Now, the Defence have submitted this because this is a crucial time. On the 16th and the 18th of April, the Vitezovi were involved in the attack on Stari Vitez, and on the 20th of April, the Vitezovi were involved in the attack on Gacice. Now, the appellant doesn't deny that certain attacks took place. What he is says is that they were outside his command and control and that Kraljevic, the head of the Vitezovi, was basically uncontrollable and that he reported directly to Mostar. Now, the appellant has submitted this and this document has been admitted, once again just at the threshold of admissibility stage, that it's capable of belief, as indicating that this shows that the commander of the Vitezovi, which you can see at the bottom is Darko Kraljevic, that he is sending an order directly to the Main Staff in Mostar. If you see the top it says: "The head of Defence," "The Chief of the Main Staff," and then, "Colonel Primorac." The argument is that this evidence would demonstrate that the Vitezovi does not report to General Blaskic. If I can just note one thing before I go to the new documents which the Prosecution submit should be before you. If you look in the top of the page, it says: "The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatian Community," then this comes down to "Command of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, Vitez Forward Command Post." The argument of the appellant is that this was done obviously without Blaskic's knowledge and it was done directly from Mostar. The forward command post is Blaskic's forward command post, and the forward command post at this time is in the Hotel Vitez, which is General Blaskic's headquarters. So it's coming actually from the headquarters of General Blaskic, the forward command post which is stationed within it. If I can ask you to turn over to page 76, please. The Prosecution puts this document before you simply as background. This is a trial exhibit. This is trial Exhibit P666. This trial exhibit indicates that the Vitezovi are attached to Blaskic in January 1993. There was testimony before the Court that that attachment was never removed by Blaskic's superior. If I can ask you to turn over to page 79, please. This is also a trial exhibit, just to put in context order that you've admitted. This trial exhibit indicates that on April 15th, there's a preparatory combat command order, and it's a direct order from General Blaskic to the Vitezovi on April 15th. You'll see at the end of the page what's essentially paragraph 2, it states: "Assignment Of Our Forces." And then on the next page it indicates what the assignment is to the Vitezovi. If you turn over to page 83, please. Once again, this is just to put it in context. This is a trial exhibit. And on April 15, 1993, the same time as the order by General Blaskic, the second paragraph reads: "The Vitezovi unit is, as the name indicates, a special unit which is, in the unified system of command and control in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone..." Now, these were the documents at trial. It's the backdrop of specific orders assigning tasks to the Vitezovi by General Blaskic. Now, the material you have before you, including Exhibit 88, is material about the criminal nature of the head of the Vitezovi and some orders, number 88 being the one that I drew your attention to because it's on April 17th, right between the two attacks on Stari Vitez in which the Vitezovi was involved. If I can ask you to turn to page 90, please. This is a document which the Prosecution submits should be before you for your determination as to whether you would order a new trial. This is a report from the head of the Vitezovi to Mostar. It's a report from Darko Kraljevic to the Main Staff in Mostar. This is on April the 26th, 1993. I'd ask you to make specific note of the first paragraph. "In the treacherous army attack of the army of BH - in other words the Muslim forces - on everything that is Croatian, on orders from the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, I carried out the following combat operations." If you look down there, you will see April 16th, April 17th, April 18th, April 19th, April 20th, 21st, 22nd, all the way down to the 25th. You will recall that the attacks in Stari Vitez and in Gacice were on the 16th, the 18th, and the 20th of April. This report, which of course goes to Mostar, he does report his tasks back to Mostar, but it's purely a reporting function. This indicates that he was by orders of Blaskic carrying out combat operations, specifically the dates that the crimes were committed at a time when General Blaskic indicated that they were not under his command or control and he had no authority over them. If you turn over to page 93 of the same document, you'll see in the middle of the page in the paragraph the last sentence of the paragraph in the middle of the page it says: "Regarding the Vitezovi, it is best that you read the written commendation from the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, Tihomir Blaskic, which I am sending you." It's rather odd that somebody who has no authority and no idea what they're doing is actually writing them a commendation in the middle of April during the conflict. Lastly, I ask you to turn over to page 98. This is a report from General Blaskic to the Main Staff in Mostar. It's on the 22nd of June, 1993, and it relates to the Vitezovi. If you turn to the second page of that report, specifically page 99 at the bottom, Your Honours. It says in the middle, the beginning of the second full paragraph: "I should mention that the Vitezovi Battalion has, in fact, performed all its assigned combat tasks." It's a little odd that General Blaskic is reporting on combat tasks which he indicates and says that he can't assign. At the bottom of the page it says: "I know that the unit is made up of young men, who sometimes kick over the trace as little, but I know that the unit command is on top of the situation and has absolute control over the entire formation of the unit," and the next part I stress, "and that all Central Bosnia Operative Zone commands are carried out in their entirety, without arguments and on time." My respectful submission, if you had these documents before you and if you were to receive submissions from the Prosecution on these issues, you would not find that a new trial is warranted on the basis of the documents that are before you that have been admitted in the 47 documents. In fact, the document which is relied on, Exhibit 88, where the head of the Vitezovi is reporting to the Main Staff is equally consistent with the fact that they report to the Main Staff. They also take their logistical supplies from the Main Staff. I note that there are a number of reports or orders put in where their request for logistical supplies for the Vitezovi from the Main Staff. If you look at Exibit D250 at trial, you'll see that the Vitezovi report in their annual report that they get their logistics from the Main Staff. With respect, based on these documents, the material filed by the appellant would certainly not warrant a new trial. If I may in the last 15 minutes simply go to the other matters that I indicated I would address. One of the issues which is set out in the Scheduling Order is whether the sheer volume of the material warrants a new trial. I respectfully submit that it's not so voluminous. It's 47 documents and two witnesses. At this moment, I appreciate, of course, that there are more documents which this Chamber has reserved on, of course. But at this point in time, based on the premise under which we're proceeding is that the 47 documents and two witnesses warrants a new trial. I have already referred to the sheer volume of material dealt with in the Kupreskic Appeals Chamber, and I appreciate the hardship that that put them under, but that matter was dealt with. The complexity of the case, well I'm sure the Appeals Chamber has dealt with more complex issues than this one. In the Celebici appeal, the proceedings were much more extensive and the issues were very complex. The Appeals Chamber has also dealt with the complexity of additional evidence in Tadic where it dealt with 80 witness statements, in Kupreskic, which I've already referred to, in Kambanda where they heard testimony for a full day from Mr. Kambanda himself, from Musema where they called an additional evidence hearing. Second, most of the material before you at this point, 47 are documents. With respect, the Trial Chamber is in no different position than you are when it comes to documents. You assess the documents. You determine whether they fit and whether they're consistent with the evidence that's presently on the record, and you considered them in relation to the evidence on the record. If there are any issues that could go to credibility if documents have to be put to witness, that can be dealt with by this court. There's only two witnesses at this point in time who are indicated as being necessary to be called. Even assuming that the Prosecution calls, take an estimate, eight witnesses in response, that's only ten witnesses. And even if it adds two documents for every one that the Defence has, that's, let's say, 100 documents, I don't see any reason why this Court couldn't deal with 100 documents and ten witnesses in three to four weeks, as opposed to sending it back for a new trial that would take 25 months. The Appeals Chamber may consider the fact that it's not its function to hear evidence, it's not a fact-finding body, and that's certainly been expressed in some of the previous decisions, but 115 grants it that authority and it's undertaken that task extensively in the past. The Kupreskic Appeals Chamber specifically permits it to send it back to a Trial Chamber to determine the additional evidence, if it's not in a position. There's no authority in Kupreskic, and it certainly doesn't warrant sending it back on new trial on the basis of Rule -- Article 25 of the Statute that there was an error when there's been no determination that the facts, in fact, would lead to an error. There is, at least, an assumption that there would be a requirement for a rehearing of the entire case, and it's the Prosecution's submission that that's certainly not the case. I've handed out to the senior legal officer -- he doesn't have to hand it up at this time, it's just for your information, I've given one to counsel for the appellant -- a chart of five pages long of counts or subparts of counts which are not affected by the additional evidence. You have to remember that this is a case that stemmed over a 14-month campaign, and 20 villages, of three municipalities, and regarding all kinds of crimes. And the chart which I've indicated sets out those ones which are purely illustrative. They're just examples of counts or subparts of counts which are not affected by the additional evidence that's been admitted, and the Prosecution submits that there should be further submissions on this as the Prosecution would make further submissions on the issue of whether the counts are affected and I'll ask, if you wish, that the senior legal officer give it to you at a later time. Lastly, there are counts that the Prosecution submits should not be sent back for trial even if there is additional evidence and, once again, the Prosecution submits that you should hear the Prosecution's evidence in rebuttal, and material should be tested. But even if that's not the case, you should hear supplemental submissions as envisioned in the previous order. One of the counts is -- relates to the Vitez municipality and relates to Gacice, and in that case, the victims, the civilians from Gacice, in one of three specific aspects of the events there, were taken specifically to the Hotel Vitez which is Blaskic's headquarters. They were placed around the Hotel Vitez for three hours to prevent shelling of the headquarters of General Blaskic. The evidence at trial was that for 20 hours the day before, on the 19th, there was shelling of the Hotel Vitez and shelling of Vitez and, therefore, these victims were brought there, 247 were placed around the headquarters of General Blaskic. The testimony at trial was that he left at some point in time in the late afternoon to go to a meeting in Zenica. The war diary is the new evidence now admitted by this Chamber for the purpose of demonstrating that there should be a different finding on that issue. The war diary indicates that General Blaskic left for Zenica at 1650, ten to 5.00 in the afternoon. That's exactly what the Trial Chamber essentially found. The Trial Chamber didn't find that wasn't -- he didn't go to Zenica. The Trial Chamber found he was there for the afternoon during the time, that he left late in the afternoon. Yes, the war diary is submitted by the appellants affect the evidence or is relevant to one of the counts, but with respect, it makes no difference. In the Prosecution's submission, it would be beneficial, in the least, if the Appeals Chamber was to hear submissions on these specific issues before it takes the next step. In closing, it's the Prosecution's submission that it's premature at this stage to order a new trial as required by the procedural law of this Tribunal, the Rules, and basically common sense when you consider the practical considerations. This Chamber can perform that task and make an informed decision before it proceeds. I wonder whether the Appeals Chamber would do the same if it was an acquittal that was being challenged. On the basis of additional evidence, after a 25-month trial that is untested, no arguments on it, and no evidence in rebuttal, would the Appeals Chamber order that an acquittal is overturned and order a new trial on the basis of the number of documents that were before it and two witnesses which have been unchallenged? I would respectfully submit it wouldn't be the appropriate course. If you consider the evidence as, in the Prosecution's submission, you should, and as indicated by Kupreskic, you will conclude that much of the appellant's evidence is full of contradictions and unsubstantiated inferences and that many of the factual bases upon which they are asking that a new trial will be ordered will reveal that will be nothing more than a facade. Those are my submissions at the moment, Your Honours. I'm -- obviously have eight more minutes for questions; if not, I'm concluded with the Prosecution's submissions on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Farrell, you said that we had authority under Rule 115 to refer to a Trial Chamber the issues which arise under that Rule. The Rule itself doesn't say so, but are you relying, for example, upon the Celebici decision to refer such a type of matter to a Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: No, I may have misspoke there. The reliance is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. specifically on the Kupreskic Appeals Chamber judgement, paragraph 70, where it indicates that, "The Appeals Chamber can test the evidence itself or order the case to be remitted to a Trial Chamber to hear the new evidence." That's the passage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I am grateful to see that there is some support for the Celebici judgement that was so strongly challenged on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL

I presume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So we can resume our hearing. I give the floor to counsel for the appellant for 75 minutes. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and thank you for the opportunity to address these issues here today with the Appeals Chamber. The fundamental problem in this case is one that the Prosecution is responsible for, and that is that they chose to bring the indictment in this case at a time when they did not have access to the war archive of the HVO or the BH army. They chose to bring a case of command responsibility against then, at the time of the war, Colonel Blaskic, who was responsible for the Bosnian Croat militia area of responsibility within Central Bosnia, and the prosecution was undertaken without either the complete archive of the HVO militia, the Bosnian Croat militia, or the archive of the BH army, that is the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was the successor, if you will, to a large extent to the Territorial Defence or TO forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So the prosecution was undertaken, if you will, with a relative lack of access to the most important evidence in the case, because in a case, I submit to you, of command responsibility, it is very important what the orders flowing down from the commander are and what the reports flowing up to the commander are. It is very important what documents like the war diary show. What was the information that the commander had available to him? This case was prosecuted without that material, and that was a decision that the Prosecution made. The result has been this tortured, if you will, appellate proceeding to date where documents have been dribbling in. We have filed three Rule 115 motions, as the Court is aware. We're continuing to get more documents from the Prosecution under Rule 68. They have told us they're reviewing another 1.4 million pages of documents. This is in the court record. They filed their correspondence with Your Honours. And they believe 25.000 pages of that material are likely to be directly relevant to General Blaskic and his area of command during the civil war. So here we are. Here we are. Meanwhile, General Blaskic has been in prison for six and a half years. The Prosecution feels it's premature to remand this case for a new trial. We do not think it is premature, and we ask the Appeals Chamber to act with due speed to remand this case for a new trial. My learned colleague first addressed the question of whether Your Honours have the authority to remand the case for a new trial. I disagree with my learned colleague. Both Article 25 of the Tribunal Statute and Rule 117 (C) give Your Honours authority to remand a case on appeal to a Trial Chamber for a new trial, and that authority was recognised in the Jelisic Appeals decision, in paragraph 73, where that opinion expressly acknowledged that Your Honours have the discretion to order a retrial. Rule 117 does not limit that ability, and I submit to you that Rule 115 does not limit that ability. If you look at Rule 115 and the cases applying it and interpreting it, none of these cases say that this Court, in accepting a 115 motion to admit new evidence, is somehow locked into a process or a procedure which it must pursue for months and months and months without making an ultimate decision in a case, particularly whereas here the appellate briefs were filed months ago. Your Honours have the appellate briefs. You have our three Rule 115 motions. You have ruled on approximately 50 items in those Rule 115 motions. You have a tremendous amount of information before you. All of those processes have been duly pursued and Your Honours have given it great attention. So we disagree with the Prosecution that you don't have the authority and that it's premature to act in this appeal. The Kupreskic appellate decision does not differ, we submit, from that analysis. Paragraph 70 of that opinion states, in essence, that once an Appeals Chamber find there is relevant -- finds - excuse me - there is relevant 115 evidence, you have two choices. You can weigh it yourselves, or you can send it back to the Trial Chamber -- to a Trial Chamber. It doesn't limit what -- for what purpose you can send it back. You can send it to a Trial Chamber for retrial, we submit, and we submit that that is included within the analysis described at paragraph 70 of the Kupreskic appellate decision. That's all I'm going to say about your authority. You have the authority to do it, and the Defence calls upon you in this case to act pursuant to that authority. Should you order a retrial based on the newly admitted 115 evidence? That is the question you asked us to address. That is the question I will focus on. The Defence submits that you should do so for three independent reasons, and I will list them and then address them in order. First, the content or substance of the newly admitted evidence requires a retrial. Second, procedural fairness in this case requires that a fair trial be held. The first trial was not a fair trial for reasons I will enumerate, so we need a new trial for procedural fairness. Third, the efficient process of justice requires a new trial. First, what about the new evidence and its contents? Well, the standard articulated in the Jelisic decision is that this Court can remand for a new trial if it's in the interests of justice. And the Jelisic appellate decision enumerates some of those factors, but I believe they are illustrative not exclusive, and I will address at some length, in my comments, why it is in the interests of justice for a new trial to occur. To understand the meaning of the new evidence, we need to step back from the analysis that my learned colleague undertook. He looked at a few orders, made some interesting comments that I will respond to in due course. But I ask you to step back for a moment, look at the new evidence in it's totality and at it's core what the new evidence tells Your Honours about the crimes in Ahmici, where horrible crimes occurred and more than 100 civilians - men, women and children - lost their lives in the early morning of April 16th, 1993. The Trial Chamber was faced with a situation where there were no illegal orders by the accused. How did the Trial Chamber reach its judgement? And again, I have great empathy for the Trial Chamber acting in the relative vacuum in which it was forced to act by the Prosecutor's hand. The Trial Chamber reasoned as follows: Colonel Blaskic had effective control over all the HVO troops in the Lasva Valley. Crimes were committed by those troops that were organised and had to be organised and orchestrated by some supervisory or directing authority. Therefore, the Trial Chamber concluded Colonel Blaskic must have organised, directed, and orchestrated those crimes because he was the superior authority. He was the only superior authority over those troops in the Lasva Valley. That is the thesis of the judgement. The Trial Chamber went on to evaluate the rest of the evidence within this framework. It found, for example, because they didn't have all of Colonel Blaskic's orders, they inferred that some of the missing orders were likely illegal orders to commit crimes. That's in the judgement at paragraphs 589 and 590. They didn't have access to the archives. They couldn't go and see what were the orders issued between Thursday and Saturday. If they had, they could have gone and looked at those orders and seen that there were no illegal orders. The Trial Chamber also reasoned that with respect to the critical issue of Ahmici and whether he ordered the crimes, and whether, thereafter, he attempted to diligently investigate who had committed those crimes so that they could be brought to justice, the Trial Chamber found that Colonel Blaskic was not able to produce a copy of the investigative report by the Bosnian Croat Security and Information Service or SIS which he claimed, and he did testify and say he directed SIS to investigate Ahmici, the Trial Chamber found because Colonel Blaskic wasn't able to produce that report - and I believe the Trial Chamber called it the single one most important piece of evidence that Colonel Blaskic could have produced to clear his name - the Trial Chamber found that failure, "Cast doubt on the very existence of such a report." I am quoting from the judgement at paragraph 493. I'll return to the existence or nonexistence of that report in a moment. That's the essential framework of the judgement. Our thesis is that the archival evidence breaks the chain of logic in the Trial Chamber's reasoning. It breaks it in several important areas. First -- well, let's return to the report. We have the SIS report, the investigative report into the crimes in Ahmici. It corroborates not only that there was an investigation, that there was a report prepared, the report is dated in November of 1993, which is about the right time given the attempts by appellant, repeated attempts to have an investigation conducted. But the report exonerates the appellant. It identifies the perpetrators of the crime in Ahmici and exonerates him. Imagine how different the trial would have been below if we had been able to get that report and produce it to the Trial Chamber. Instead of inferring that his failure to get it indicated his guilt, the Trial Chamber would have known he pursued it, he had it investigated. The perpetrators were identified, they were reported, by the way, not to him, but to the political leadership in Bosnia in Herzegovina. That is the Croatian, the Bosnian Croat political leadership in Mostar as well as President Tudjman in Zagreb who did nothing to bring the real perpetrators to justice. Only this court has taken steps, meaningful steps, to bring the real perpetrators to justice. But what is the importance of the new evidence? Let me step back from the SIS investigative report of Ahmici and proceed a little more analytically. First of all, the new evidence indicates that Colonel Blaskic did not have effective control over the two key special units operating in the Lasva Valley and they were the 4th Battalion of the military police, and the Vitezovi unit. Why is this very important? This is very important because most of the units, most of the brigades based in towns were made up of villagers with very little by way of military training, very little by way of arms. They were not -- they were in the nature of a village militia, not in the nature of army troops as we, in the west, tend to think of them. By contrast, the Vitezovi and the military police 4th Battalion, particularly the Jokers unit, they were young men, they had special pay, they had special weapons, they had training, and they answered directly to elements outside of the Lasva Valley. The military police unit answered to the military police administration in Mostar, and the Vitezovi answered to the Ministry of Defence in Mostar. That's how they got their special pay, their special logistics, their special weapons. So they, in a sense, were the most capable fighting forces in the region. However, these units were made up of young men and they were headed by criminals. Darko Kraljevic, who headed the Vitezovi, was someone who acted on his own will and there were various -- I will refer to a couple of incidents but he was someone who was out of control in ordinary parlance. The military police, meanwhile, particularly the 4th Battalion, as I'm speaking of, and the Jokers, they had a line to the military police administration in Mostar, but they actually had a very close relationship with the political figure in Busovaca. Most of the men in the Jokers unit of the military police came from Busovaca, and that man was Dario Kordic. So what is the evidence? What is the new evidence about the ability of Colonel Blaskic to have effective control over the military police? Well, the intelligence reports that we have provided to you detail that the military police acted at their own initiative, on their own adventures or misadventures. For example, Exhibit 10 to our first Rule 115 motion: Two other witnesses speak very clearly to this and these are witnesses that testified for the Prosecutor from the Kordic trial. General Merdan, a General in the BH army testified that Colonel Blaskic could not control Darko Kraljevic and the Vitezovi. Indeed, it was viewed as a laughable proposition, as I recall. Similarly the information officer for the Vitezovi testified in the Kordic case. His name is Ante Breljas. He testified that Kraljevic did what he wanted. If he wanted to go along with whatever, if there was a military operation that Colonel Blaskic wanted to pursue, he would go with it if he wanted, and if he didn't, he wouldn't. And if he wanted to do his own action on his own initiative, he would do that also.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We have reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. After all these years, the case is still exciting. So we have General Merdan, Mr. Breljas, intelligence reports all informing us, if you will, that although at times the Vitezovi did act in concert with other HVO units, the Trial Chamber was not in a position to assume that Colonel Blaskic had effective control over the Vitezovi at all times, and that is the assumption they made in the three-step logic that I outlined earlier. Now, there were some comments by my colleague about the Vitezovi specifically, and I believe he tendered to Your Honours in one of his filings some additional and new documents relating to the Vitezovi, and one of them is a report from this Kraljevic who headed the Vitezovi saying, "During this period of time I did all these things acting on Colonel Blaskic's orders." This isn't a mini-trial, and I don't want to spend a lot of time responding to these discrete documents, but I can't resist responding to these few. First of all, note that the reports were sent to the Main Staff in Mostar. What is the Vitezovi unit doing reporting to the Main Staff in Mostar if they're truly subordinated to Colonel Blaskic in Vitez? One of the documents is a protest to the BH army. Mr. Kraljevic is sending his own protest to the enemy forces, speaking directly to them, not through any command structure either in Mostar or in Vitez. He's having his own dialogue with the enemy. That would be insubordination in any normal configuration or army. Also, if you look at all these documents authored by Mr. Kraljevic, leader of the Vitezovi, you will see that Colonel Blaskic isn't copied on any of them. He wasn't privy to any of those communications. Mr. Kraljevic considered him largely irrelevant. Mr. Kraljevic carried on his own dialogue with his superior command in Mostar, with enemy forces, et cetera. So the new evidence speaks to a lack of effective control over the military police and the Jokers. It speaks to a lack of effective control by Colonel Blaskic over the Vitezovi. It also speaks to the situation in Kiseljak. If you haven't seen a map, it's very instructive. During this relevant period of the war, there was a small enclave around Vitez a mile or two across. There was a larger enclave around Kiseljak, and there's a road connecting them, and a few -- a hundred yards on either side of the road was controlled by the HVO. So in the nature of a dumbbell, if you will, with one end of the dumbbell larger than the other. The road to Kiseljak and in between -- and there's a third little circle, essentially Busovaca. The road to Kiseljak was cut in January of 1993 by the BH army, and thereafter, Colonel Blaskic could not travel to Kiseljak other than with the help of UNPROFOR. So my learned colleague showed you a couple of reports, additional reports I think that we've tendered, to show that despite the fact that he was cut off, Colonel Blaskic continued to send humanitarian orders to Kiseljak, and we tendered the additional follow-up, if you will, disseminating orders by the commander down there to show you that these were real orders issued by Colonel Blaskic. They weren't orders issued with a wink and a nod. They were serious orders, and they were apparently repeated in those instances. Nonetheless, if you look at the new evidence that we've submitted, with respect to Kiseljak first of all, there is an EC monitor by the name of Witness AO or AD, I believe it's AD, who testified again in the Kordic case that Blaskic didn't have reliable information about events in Kiseljak or the other far-flung enclaves, and he could not control HVO troops in those far-flung, cut-off, disparate enclaves. The new evidence also shows that the person who became the commander in Kiseljak, Ivica Rajic, he reported directly to the Main Staff in Mostar because he could travel to Mostar, whereas those in the Lasva Valley, such as Colonel Blaskic, could not travel by land to Mostar. So the new evidence also addresses the question of whether Colonel Blaskic had effective control over HVO troops in Kiseljak, and that evidence speaks clearly that he did not. But that is just the beginning of it, Your Honours. Not only does the new evidence show that these units, particularly the military police and the Vitezovi, acted on their own will and at their own initiative, but other elements outside of the de jure chain of command exerted control over the military police, particularly the Jokers, and I'm referring to Dario Kordic. What evidence am I speaking of? Well, if you look at Exhibits 4 and 5 to our Rule 115 motion, you will find reports authored for President Tudjman of Croatia by the Croatian intelligence service written in February of 1994. February of 1994 is long before Colonel Blaskic was ever charged with anything in connection with this case, to my knowledge. Those intelligence reports which, by the way, do cite statements having been taken from witnesses and so forth, state unequivocally who is responsible for the crimes in Ahmici, and it states that Dario Kordic and another man named Ignac Kostroman, who was also a political figure in the Busovaca area of Central Bosnia, were responsible for directing and ordering the massacre. It goes on to say that Colonel Blaskic had little influence, if any, over military operations designed by Kordic and Kostroman. Now, rather than speak to the issue of Ahmici and the impact of the new evidence concerning who actually ordered those crimes, the Prosecutor nibbles at the edges and ridicules the statement in this HIS report that the Vitez Brigade was not in Ahmici. Now, this is an important point, in all fairness to the Prosecutor, because the military police acted on orders of others and the Vitez Brigade was more of a village brigade without this exotic relationship, if you will, with a political figure in Busovaca. However, if you look at the reports that my colleague has cited to, they are in the nature generally of general reports from the Vitez Brigade reporting on activity in their entire geographic area, that is the Vitez municipality. One of them lists 15 different locations where there's fighting going on. The Vitez Brigade was not in all those places. They were making a report of the geographic area of the Vitez municipality to their commander. I also note that although it is interesting for the Prosecutor to still be arguing that the Vitez Brigade was in Ahmici, the Kordic Trial Chamber found they were not in Ahmici until the afternoon of April 16, 1993, long after the massacre was committed. Indeed, the commander of the Vitez Brigade Mario Cerkez, he was acquitted for any involvement or role in the Ahmici massacre. So it is a little perplexing why the Prosecutor is still beating this drum to defend its conviction of the accused based on the ground that the Vitez Brigade somehow participated in the massacre in Ahmici which by all accounts occurred between 5.30 and 7.00 or 7.30 in the morning on the 16th of April, 1993. And lastly on this point because it is a bit of a tangent, if you look at the war diary which the Prosecutor pooh-poohs, all the reports from the Vitez Brigade on the morning of April 16th are from areas in the Vitez town area or other areas where they were assigned in the orders for defence that were issued prior to the 16th. There were no reports reflected in the war diary for the Operative Zone from the Vitez Brigade from Ahmici on the morning of April 16th. That's the value of contemporaneous evidence, evidence produced as a matter of business practice or military practice contemporaneously at a time when the events, in fact, were unknown, how the events would unfold is unknown. So I was speaking to the HIS reports, that is Hrvatska Intelligence Service, H-I-S, which is the Croatian intelligence service, prepared for President Tudjman in February of 1994. They are important evidence, we submit. But there is more. The first exhibit to our second Rule 115 motion provides even more detail about the planning and implementation of the massacre in Ahmici. This is a report prepared by the Ministry of Interior or the MUP, M-U-P in Croatia. This report details how late in the evening, the evening of April 15th to 16th, there was a clandestine meeting at the home of Dario Kordic in Busovaca attended by the leadership of the Jokers and the military police, and at that meeting, a decision was made to cause a massacre in Ahmici so as to scare the Muslim population out of the Lasva Valley. That appears to have been the perverse and criminal motive for this crime. That decision, as set forth in this report, was taken without the knowledge of and with no involvement of Colonel Blaskic who was at his military headquarters in Vitez. He was not at that meeting. He was not mentioned at that meeting. He had no involvement in that meeting. So our thesis is the new evidence breaks key links in the logic, the chain of logical conclusions that the Trial Chamber reached which unfortunately were reached because of the relative vacuum of particularly documentary information that the Trial Chamber was forced to deal with. Does this evidence require a new trial? I've already spoken to the fact that we believe that the jurisprudence of this Tribunal would permit it, certainly under the Jelisic opinion. And we also submit that this would most appropriately occur before a Trial Chamber, because as this Court has opined, I think in different settings, Trial Chambers exist to make findings of fact. Findings of fact are entitled to deference by an Appeals Chamber. There is a reason to have extensive finding -- fact-finding proceedings in a Trial Chamber, not to mention to preserves the right of appeal, which I'll speak of at greater length in a few minutes. The Rome treaty also provides for a retrial in Articles 83 and 84. Civil law countries provide for a retrial, we believe in these circumstances such as the German Code of Criminal Procedure at section 354 which provides that if questions of fact are raised, that are significant and material, the case should be remanded for a new trial. The UK Criminal Appeals Act of -- Section 2, turning to the common law, similarly provides that if a conviction is unsafe, the UK Appeals Court may either acquit or order a retrial. Both the McNamee and Clegg cases, which I think were cited by both parties, illustrate that proposition as well as the quantum of new evidence to justify a remand for a new trial. We submit that the quantum of new important exculpatory evidence already admitted here in the case of these 50 items exceeds that discussed in both of those cases. Now, the Prosecutor raises an objection to this and he says, well, but the evidence hasn't been tested, so it's premature. You can't act because the evidence hasn't been tested. Well, what is the new evidence? First of all, most, if not all of the new documents are from the Croatian War Archives in Zagreb. They bear the stamp in the upper right corner, that little circular stamp of the archives. The Kupreskic Appellate Chamber already found that documents have an official source such as that archive, those documents are -- have -- do bear the reliability and credibility of documents coming from such an official source. I hasten to conclude that if the Prosecution had any doubts that any of the documents that bear the stamp of the archive that we have submitted truly didn't come from the archive, you would have heard about it a long time ago. I also submit that Your Honours, as professional Judges, when you look at new documents, you read statements from newly proffered witnesses, and you see that this material is interlocking. It touches upon each other. It corroborates each other in different ways; some very important points, some minuscule points that no one would ever think of in trying, if they were trying to fabricate something that as professional Judges. You know it when you see it. You have a sense, having looked at these materials, read these witness statements, is this something that somebody has made up somewhere or is there a significant element of truth and reality to it? If you are satisfied that there is that element of truth and reality to it, then I submit it's been tested. It's been tested by the experience and judgement of Your Honours. So we believe the new evidence requires a retrial. We also believe that a fair trial needs to be held, and a fair trial was not held in this case. And that is an independent reason for a remand and for a new trial. First of all, two states acted affirmatively, acted to undermine the accused defence. Article 29 of the Tribunal Statute requires states to assist this Tribunal. That did not happen here in the case of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. For example, the Trial Chamber, during the trial, subpoenaed Bosnia-Herzegovina for the war diary of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone HVO. The BH authorities did not produce it. Later, everybody got it from the war archive; the Prosecutor got it, and we got it, and it's very important. It confirms the absence of illegal orders by the accused. It shows he had no knowledge of the elicit clandestine meeting at Kordic's home on the night of April 15, 16 where the massacre of Ahmici was planned, and it's useful for a number of other exculpatory reasons. But what's important for the moment is the BH authorities didn't provide this when it was subpoenaed by the Trial Chamber, and that's not fair. Colonel Blaskic was entitled to have that document here at his trial. Similarly, the Prosecutor subpoenaed the Republic of Croatia for HVO war records. We all believed they would be very relevant. Croatia did not, in the main, produce those documents. They certainly did not produce the documents that we are now able to tender to you from the archives, and they did it to protect their President, Franjo Tudjman, who had a hand in the dealings of the political leadership in Herzegovina, that is the Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are having trouble keeping up, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. So although Mr. Nobilo and I laboured hard and long to gather the relevant documents for the defence of our client, we had two secret services working against us, the Croatian SIS and the BH intelligence service, and they obstructed the defence of our client, and that was not fair. The Prosecutor also withheld key exculpatory information from us. In pursuing their case against Dario Kordic, they developed significant material tending to show that Dario Kordic exercised military authority. That material was exculpatory to Colonel Blaskic, and it was withheld. Seven of the exhibits you have admitted are from the Kordic trial. None were disclosed to the accused by the Prosecution prior to the judgement. We had to go to the Registrar's office and dig them out post-judgement. And what does that evidence go to? This is not inconsequential evidence. (redacted) Witness BA1, who testified in the Kordic proceedings that the Jokers unit of the military police were instruments of the political leadership of the Bosnian Croats. Witness AD, whom I referenced earlier, the EC monitor testified that Colonel Blaskic did not have effective control over the Kiseljak HVO because he was isolated and separate from them; Mr. Breljas, whom I mentioned; General Merdan, whom I think I mentioned, both testified in the Kordic case. If we had been given their statements in a timely manner, we believe we could have presented that important testimony to the Trial Chamber, but we didn't get it. In fact, we haven't gotten their witness statements to this day; the Prosecutor will not produce them. The Prosecutor even used a chart adopted by General Merdan in that case in which there are different boxes showing the chain of command of the Bosnian Croats, and Colonel Blaskic is down here. He's on a line below the Vitezovi, the military police, and the Kiseljak HVO.
