It is represented on that chart that Colonel Blaskic did not command any of those three elements, and they used that chart in the Kordic case to get a conviction against Kordic and didn't produce it to us, so we couldn't use it in our defence of our client. That was not fair. Included in our book of authorities are various cases providing that, in a situation where exculpatory information is withheld, a reversal and a remand for a new trial is appropriate. I'm referring to the Kyles case of the Supreme Court of the United States, and the Pelullo case. I note also that that case law speaks to the question of: Do you evaluate each piece of evidence in isolation when asking whether an accused's right to a fair trial was undermined materially or do you evaluate the cumulative effect of evidence that was improperly withheld? Kyles speaks to it. It's the cumulative effect of the inappropriately withheld evidence that should be weighed, and I submit it's persuasive. It's obviously not an authority governing this Court, but we submit it is a persuasive view. And finally, a fair trial would have required and requires that the accused had this body of helpful exculpatory information both from the war archives and from the Prosecutor's files, and that we had it to effectively examine and confront the witnesses that came forward to testify against Colonel Blaskic. And I'll give you one example, if I may. There was a witness who testified at the trial, a very nice man, an EC monitor from a Scandinavian country by the name of Lars Baggesen. He testified in this room on August 22nd, 1997. I was here. I remember it well. Mr. Baggesen said among other things -- by the way, he spent three months in Central Bosnia as an EC monitor. He gave an opinion that Colonel Blaskic controlled the military police in Central Bosnia. And we asked him: What is your basis for that conclusion? And he said, "Well, I was once detained by the military police of the HVO and -- along with General Merdan of the BH army, and after a phone call from Blaskic, I was released. So they obviously followed Blaskic's order to release me so I therefore conclude Blaskic controlled them." Well, General Merdan, as I said, he testified in the Kordic case. What did General Merdan say about this incident because he was there along with the EC monitor, Mr. Baggesen. General Merdan, who spoke the language and understood who was being said at least on the half of the phone conversation that he overheard, he testified in Kordic that the military police disregarded Blaskic's directive to release the EC monitor and Merdan, and the military police said they were waiting to hear from somebody else other than Blaskic. So to have a fair trial, it's not just a couple of witnesses or half a dozen witnesses or ten witnesses who need to be brought before this Court. Witnesses like Mr. Baggesen need to come back because Mr. Baggesen is going to recant his testimony. He's going to say, "I'm sorry, I didn't understand what was being spoken on the phone. I reached the wrong conclusion. I apologise." And there are lots of other witnesses who testified, gave opinion testimony, which was relied on very heavily by the Trial Chamber. So lots and lots of those witnesses are going to need to come back. And I'll turn in a moment to the question of should they come here before Your Honours or should there be a new trial, a fair trial, which then preserves the accused's right to have an appeal from the result of a fair trial. There's a third independent reason there should be a new trial, and that is the efficient administration of justice requires it. I don't agree with my learned colleague across the well concerning the volume of new evidence that is going to need to be assessed in order for there to be a proper and just proceeding in this case. What do we have? We have the 50 new items Your Honours have admitted. We have 100 or 200 more items that you have not yet ruled on. We have items that the Prosecutor has given us that we're still reviewing under Rule 68. It takes time. Some of them have to be translated and the like. We have the 25.000 documents which they're still reviewing. That's a subset of the 1.4 million pages of documents. Certainly we're going to be seeing some more documents from that tranche of material. We only in September this year gained access to the closed-session material from the Lasva Valley cases that's filed in the Registrar's office. We are still reviewing that for exculpatory material. We have the two witnesses whose statements we've tendered and you have agreed to hear. We have the Kordic witnesses I have referred to, BA1, Breljas, Witness AD, et cetera. And we have key witnesses from the trial that would need to come back and be given the opportunity to amend particularly their opinion testimony concerning the chain of command in the Lasva Valley with respect to the HVO. That's a lot of material. That's a lot of witnesses. Furthermore, for there to be a fair proceeding in this case, that body of material must be weighed and considered in conjunction with the trial evidence itself. We are not suggesting that the trial evidence be disregarded. The Defence has a lot of confidence that there is a lot of truth in the trial evidence despite the fact we didn't have the war archives to draw upon. So in a fair proceeding, all that material, new and old, must be weighed, considered, compared, and judged. The trial was fairly long. I believe the Prosecutor had 75 days of testimony, we had 60 days of testimony, and there are more than a thousand exhibits. So there's a lot of material there to be weighed. What is the most efficient and fairest process for that weighing and synthesis to embody or constitute? We submit that it is a process, and I'm not sure that the Prosecutor disagrees. It's not something Your Honours can do back in your Chambers. You could stack up all the transcripts and you could stack up all the documents, but they don't just merge and spit out the truth. There has to be a process. There has to be a process. And we submit that that's a process that involves adversarial parties probing, pushing, pulling for the truth, examining and cross-examining witnesses, showing witnesses documents. It's called a trial. It's not called a Rule 115 hearing. It's not called taking the matter under submission in Chambers. It is called a trial. And we are going to need a new trial so that a trier of fact can analyse, sift through, and hear this material and reach a just and fair and accurate verdict. And as I said earlier, we submit that needs to be before a Trial Chamber for the further reason that it will be such a substantial proceeding that the accused's right of appeal needs to be protected. If Your Honours hold some kind of a mini-trial or even maybe not a mini-trial, it could be a six-month trial, where is the appeal? The accused would have no right of appeal. Now, we have a lot of confidence in Your Honours, so I'm not suggesting that we are worried particularly on a practical level, but still, we think the Tribunal Statute envisions if there's to be a significant rehearing of the evidence, a new trial, call it a rehearing for six months, call it a trial for six months, it needs to be done before a Trial Chamber so that the right of appeal is preserved. Now, I'd like to try and address two more topics in my remaining time. Maybe it's only one, and that is -- no, it is two. A retrial is required on all counts, and a retrial should occur before a newly constituted Trial Chamber. But let's address first all counts. The lack of procedural fairness in the first trial infects the conviction as a whole. All counts of conviction were affected by that lack of fairness. The fact that we did not have relevant documents from two states but instead their intelligence services actively worked against us, the fact that we did not have relevant exculpatory material from the Prosecutor means that all counts should be set aside as to conviction. Further, much of the new evidence goes to the proposition of whether Colonel Blaskic had effective control over all HVO forces in the Lasva Valley. And if you accept, as we believe you must, that there is clearly reasonable doubt based on the old evidence and the new evidence, indeed there's reasonable doubt based on the new evidence alone that Colonel Blaskic did not have effective control over all such troops, then proof of a specific act by him, something he did, an order he gave or some other criminal omission is going to be required to convict him, because the next -- at the next trial, the Trial Chamber is not going to be able to assume he controlled everything done by the HVO on this terrain and therefore, if something bad happened and it had an element of organisation to it, he must have ordered it. That isn't going to work, we submit, at the next trial, so that -- so this additional level or quantum of proof is going to be required, and that infects every count. If you look at the judgement, there are no counts where the Court deviates from this effective control mode and says, "Here's an order where Colonel Blaskic ordered an attack on a village, a criminal attack, an attack on civilians." It's just not there. So we believe the effective control evidence, that is the lack of effective control evidence, affects all the counts. Now, I see a chart tendered by my colleague, and I haven't had a chance to really review it and respond. I -- my understanding was that Your Honours did not want an advocacy submission. You wanted a book of authorities and to hear our arguments orally, not to submit a brief in argument or even an argumentative chart. If the Court wishes to consider this argumentative chart, I would ask that we be given leave either to submit a reply chart or to submit a written argument explaining why we disagree with this chart, because I do disagree with this chart, but it has too many details on too many different issues to respond verbally, at least now. I may be able to do so in my rebuttal in a few minutes, but I don't believe I can do so right now. So I will turn to my last issue and then we'll still have some time for questions. And that last issue is: Should a retrial be conducted before the Trial Chamber that heard this case initially, or should it be before a newly constituted Trial Chamber? We believe a retrial should be held before a newly constituted Trial Chamber, and I'd like to make very clear that this is in no way based on any belief that the Trial Chamber in this case exhibited any bias or inappropriate feeling or belief towards the Defence or towards Colonel Blaskic. We have nothing but highest regard for the Trial Chamber Judges. We believe the Trial Chamber erred principally because it didn't have the most relevant information and evidence bearing on this case at the time it was called upon to try the case and render a verdict. In looking for what considerations the Court might review on this issue, we found a case that we thought might be instructive, and it's a United States called the Robin case, and we submitted it in our book of authorities at tab 15, and it identifies three considerations to ask in deciding whether a retrial should be before the old Judge or a new Judge. And this again is at tab 15 of our submission. Question number 1: Can the Court be reasonably expected to put out of its mind prior conclusions or evidence that should be rejected or amended? I'll read the questions and then come back to them one at a time. 2. Would reassignment advance the appearance of justice? And 3: Would reassignment entail a disproportionate waste or duplication of resources? I'll go back to the first. Could the old Trial Chamber be reasonably expected to be able to put out of its mind erroneous conclusions, testimony that may be amended by new witnesses or witnesses that come back? We submit that that would be very difficult. Hundreds of witnesses were heard. It's very difficult to keep it all straight. There also will be testimony or transcripts from some witnesses in the Kordic case. Some of the same witnesses testified in the Kordic case, et cetera. So to the extent one purpose of a new trial is a fresh look at the evidence, we think a new Trial Chamber could give the freshest look at the evidence. Secondly, we believe that assignment to a new Trial Chamber would advance the appearance of justice, which is a good thing. It builds respect for justice and for all courts and for this Tribunal. And third, would reassignment entail a disproportionate waste or duplication of resources? We submit it would not, because the original Trial Chamber cannot be reconstituted. The members of that Trial Chamber are not all still with the court. So by definition, the evidence must be heard anew, we believe. And if one Judge needs to hear it anew, the whole Trial Chamber is going to hear it anew. We looked at civil and common law on this question, and we found that civil law uniformly favours reassignment to a new trier of fact. The German, French, and Italian Codes of Criminal Procedure all indicate this at sections 354, 610 and 623 respectively. With respect to common law authorities, we found authorities in the United States. Specifically two of the Circuit Courts of Appeal have written rules or published practices to remand complex criminal cases to a new Judge, principally to promote the appearance of fairness and justice. If I may have a moment to confer with my colleagues, and then I would be pleased to entertain any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I have no further comments but would be pleased to try and answer any questions you may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayman. I turn to my colleague. Judge Guney would like to ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, you emphasised on the effect that the reporting authority was not Colonel Blaskic but the authority in Mostar. And you conclude by saying that this proved clearly that Colonel Blaskic had no effective authority to command and to control all the forces. What I would like to be enlightened on is: Do you think that different reporting authority gives enough basis in all cases to conclude that the authority in command had no effective control? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I submit, and this was our position at trial, that where you have multiple lines of authority, for example -- well, let me illustrate with the military police, the Jokers unit. They had a de jure line of reporting to the military police administration in Mostar. They were told under the military police law they also reported to Colonel Blaskic for their daily policing activities. So they had a dotted line, if you will to General Blaskic. And then we also believe, and we believe that the evidence we have been submitting and bringing to your attention also indicates that they had a de facto command relationship with Dario Kordic. So as to the Jokers and the military police, you really have three lines of command, three different lines of entities that had the ability to control the Jokers in at least some respects, although Colonel Blaskic's line was limited to daily policing activities but for any attachment or subordination, resubordination of the unit. That does not mean that it is impossible that Colonel Blaskic had effective control of that unit at any particular time. We do not maintain that. What we maintain is that if you have three lines, then what the Trial Chamber did is impermissible. You cannot assume that there's only one line and assume that anything they do is at the direction of the holder of the first line. You have to look at the facts, look at what happened, look at what was ordered, look at what was reported, who knew what to figure out if that unit committed a crime. Did they do it on their own initiative? Did they do it on the orders of Dario Kordic? Did they do it on the orders of the police administration in Mostar or did they do it on the orders of the Colonel Blaskic assuming, at that point in time, the unit was attached or subordinated to Colonel Blaskic? That is all we are maintaining. That you have to look at the specifics, you cannot assume away two out of the three potential lines of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Gunawardana, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: The Prosecutor submitted that you are seeking a retrial on the basis of untested evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: The Prosecutor submitted that you are seeking a retrial on the basis untested evidence. What liability do you attach to the items of evidence that you are relying on for asking for a retrial?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The documents, Your Honour, for the most part - and I haven't looked at every one, I can do that before the rebuttal period - are in the main from a military archive. Documents in a military archive are akin to documents created in the ordinary course of business so they have a certain inherent reliability, but you do have to look at the document and see where did the information come from. Where you have a war diary, that is something that a secretary is writing down minute by minute, based on the best information that they are hearing. If you have an intelligence report, you look at it and determine, well, what did they do? Do they know who they interviewed? Does it say on the face of the report where it came from? We submit that the documents in the main -- they are from an official archive. The Prosecutor has drawn upon them for other prosecutions. They are not going to stand up and say: We think these are documents that were not contemporaneously created during the civil war. They cannot do that. They are using these documents themselves in various cases. As for the witnesses that the Prosecutor called that we want to use in the Kordic case, Mr. Breljas, (redacted), these are those witnesses. I don't think they are going to tell you in the rebuttal period that they think those witnesses lack credibility or lack reliability. They found them sufficiently credible and reliable to present them on their own behalf in the Kordic case. And further, we have two witnesses which, as you know, Your Honours have indicated a willingness to hear their evidence. They submitted a sworn statement. At least one of the statements is self-inculpatory. It is a statement against interest which, in the system, the legal system I'm most familiar with where you make a statement against interest, it has some additional element of credibility. And then lastly, I would submit that Your Honours are receiving information, new evidence, from the many different sources and that if you can undertake a rough collation and comparison of that information, you will find, for example, that the testimony given by these witnesses in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Kordic that we would like to introduce, the testimony by the two new witnesses we would like to bring before the trier of fact, and the documents from the archive, they are all speaking essentially the same message so that there is an element of corroboration within the new evidence. Those are the ways in which we submit either they are tested or can be tested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: So you would be leading evidence to establish the authenticity of the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The -- well, the documents, at least in the main, they are from an official archive. We can bring a custodian from the archive, just as the Prosecutor can, so I don't think it's in dispute that they are official documents from the archive. The witnesses are a different matter. Witnesses need to testify and be sworn and be subject to cross-examination, but I don't think the Prosecutor feels they need to be tested now before Your Honours make any decision. We're simply saying witnesses should be tested and subject to cross-examination. But you already know enough, you have enough to conclude that there needs to be a retrial in this case, and since you know that, you should act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Hunt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, one of the factors we have to consider is, you acknowledged in that case from the United States that you cited, is the waste of resources that would be involved in a completely new trial. The length of the first trial is a rather alarming factor in that. The length of the first trial, for whatever reasons that existed which caused it, nevertheless leave me to ask you: Would the accused on this occasion be prepared to accept a great deal of the evidence which doesn't -- which isn't affected by these documents but could be just led by the tender of the transcripts?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Of course I need to speak to him on that question, Your Honour, but I would expect that a considerable amount of the testimony could be accepted on the transcripts. For example, we spent almost the first year in trial hearing from victims in different villages including survivors of the Ahmici massacre and they testified -- 98 per cent, 99 per cent of their testimony was uncontroverted. So I think there is a significant amount of testimony that could be accepted based on the transcript; however, I also think that the important testimony in the case is not the victim testimony. Villages were burned, civilians died in Ahmici. The important testimony are the individuals who had dealings with Colonel Blaskic and the members of the International Community that gave opinion testimony about the chain of command within the HVO, and those witnesses all have to come back and be retested with the new evidence. Whether that means the trial will be half as long or two thirds as long or one-third as long, I don't know, but I would note, although we went on for 24 months, there were only 135 days of trial. So -- and we only had one courtroom for much of the early period, and that's why we got one week of trial per month and so forth. So I hope that's somewhat responsive to Your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well it is, but you can understand why I ask, I think. There was, if I may say so, an element of gamesmanship in a lot of the trial that appears, even from a brief association with having read some of the material in it. The Defence, for example, was not revealed until almost, I think, when your client began to give evidence, the nature of the defence, the general nature of the defence, and it seems to me that if there were to be a new trial, there would have to be some fairly strict conditions laid. I personally would accept the qualifications you gave to your answer, but for the year, the whole year of victims' evidence, that should never be repeated. Now, you do understand that there would have to be some sort of a condition laid on a new trial that all of that evidence would have to be admitted, the transcript of it, or the findings by the first Trial Chamber subject to any particular things that you want to raise. And that would be for the new Trial Chamber to decide whether you should be entitled to have those witnesses recalled.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I agree completely, Your Honour, and I also believe that if a new trial is ordered, the Defence will sit down with the Prosecution - some of us in this room have been working on this case since 1996, it probably shows in our faces - we will sit down and have a heart to heart about how we can try this case in somewhere between three and six months and get it done. What can be reduced to a stipulation, what testimony can be simply admitted and perhaps summarised so that the Court doesn't have to read stacks and stacks of repetitive material. But I think there will be a spirit of trying to get it -- to get it done in the most efficient way possible simply because this case has gone on so long and it's taken such a big chunk out of the accused's life as well as counsel's lives, professional lives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I think this concludes this part of the hearing. We can break now for -- resume at ten to 6.00, I would say. Quarter to 6.00, quarter to 6.00 then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, we heard the presentation of the parties. We can now hear the replies. I will give the floor to the Prosecution for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, Judge Pocar. Your Honours, good afternoon. Let me start by making one general observation. I have yet to hear where the error is that would warrant a new trial. I may have been mistaken in the submissions by my learned colleague, but I have not yet heard where the Trial Chamber erred or where the evidence and facts before you results in an objectively found incorrectness of facts as required by Tadic. With respect, the requirements of the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and of the procedural law of this Tribunal cannot be circumvented simply because of the extensive nature of the document. The specific law of this Tribunal requires, as said in Kupreskic, the hearing, testing of the evidence, and a determination whether or not it affects it to the point where the test is that no reasonable tribunal of fact, on the basis all the evidence, could have rendered the decision it did. If this Chamber is hearing a motion on misconduct, which is that now you should grant a new trial because the appellant didn't have it at the time, that is a separate issue and is not subject to the Rule 115 standard and is not before you on the basis of the Rule 115 application. If we're going to change in midstream on this issue, the Prosecution submits that you should at least hear the arguments which will come before you on the appeal proper on this issue. The three apparent arguments encompassed, of course -- and my learned colleague made a number of arguments. I'm just addressing these ones. The three apparent arguments which support this allegation of misconduct or the hiding of documents which would warrant intervention at this stage is essentially a ground of appeal, in my respectful submission. This is not a determination of the 115 application stage. He, first of all, says the ABiH archives were withheld from him despite his intention and his actions. I'm sure you're aware that the ABiH archives were not received by the Prosecution until months after his trial concluded. There's no misconduct which he's insinuating in relation to the ABiH archives. There's no basis for claiming that that -- those actions are such that this Court should take the severe step and warrant a new trial on that basis without looking at the evidence and testing it. The ABiH archives, which were discovered by the Prosecution in the fall of 2000, were immediately disclosed as required which the Rules. I would note that none, and I would like to reinforce that, none of the documents admitted by this Court come from the ABiH archives. Of the 47 documents, there are none that originate from that archive. So what you have is you have a plea from the appellant based on no demonstration of misconduct, something he can raise on the appeal proper, and no documents before you from that archive. Secondly, the Croatian archives. There's been extensive litigation on the availability, and I will refrain from any comment on that. The only thing I would note is that the allegation now that there was the attempt by the Prosecution to proceed without all the evidence is, quite respectfully, irrelevant. If there's sufficient evidence to confirm this, there was, and if there's sufficient evidence to convict, and there was, the issue now can be resolved through the 115 process. The Defence at trial never once brought a motion seeking for access to the Croatian archives. The Prosecution brought many and never once did they join in the Prosecution in claiming that they were not getting access and asking for a subpoena or a court order to the State of Croatia for documents. If they wish to make some argument now, they can make it in the appeal, but this allegation is, quite frankly, of limited value. Lastly, they allege that the Prosecution has withheld evidence, and they cite, I think it's three examples. This is and can be part of their appeal. It's not even been demonstrated that these allegations are true or the evidence itself is such that it would have affected the verdict. On that basis alone, I would submit that the Court should not be using that as a basis prior to the argument of the appeal and a determination by this Appeals Chamber on the appeal on that issue as a basis for warranting a new trial. Regarding some of the comments with respect to the evidence, I won't go through it in any depth. Regarding the documents that I referred to, the Vitezovi documents, the specific documents that the commander of the Vitezovi said he was under Blaskic's orders at the material time, the Defence say when you look at all these documents, you'll see that Blaskic was actually not copied on any of them. Well, the three he's referring to are the ones at trial. The three that the Prosecution has presented today has a Blaskic order to the Vitezovi -- well, it's issued by Blaskic. There's no need that he's copied. Another is a report by Blaskic to the Main Staff about the Vitezovi. Well, the copying issue is irrelevant. And the third is a report by Kraljevic to the Main Staff where he says he's under Blaskic's orders. With respect, the allegation that's been made is unfounded. My learned colleague made reference to Rajic, this is in the additional material, it's at the end of the material, and said that this was a demonstration that they were cut off and Rajic was reporting directly to Mostar. If you remember the documents that were admitted by the Appeals Chamber about Rajic, they relate specifically to correspondence between Rajic and Mostar regarding the XY side; the XY side is the Serb side. It relates to the issue of whether or not they can get logistics from the Serb side and whether or not the -- they can get members from a Croatian area through into -- through a Serb area and into a Croatian area. Well, if you look at the two documents that are submitted in the material, Blaskic wrote the order, the request to the Main Staff for that specific issue and said that because this is at the high level between the senior staff of the Serb army and the senior staff of the HVO army, it has to be dealt with at that level, and he specifically requests that the Main Staff of Mostar deal with it. Secondly, Blaskic is cut off. He doesn't have access to the Serb area. Rajic does. You'll also see in the material that's been filed that there is a second document in which Blaskic is involved in the correspondence by Rajic to the Main Staff on this very issue. The rest of the documents, in my submission, really are not sufficient to warrant a new trial, and don't demonstrate the proposition for which they've been put forward. The appellant's counsel refers to the fact that the Prosecution seems to be continually trying to implicate Cerkez in the Ahmici crimes and that the Trial Chamber in Kordic and Cerkez found that the Vitezovi was not there. Well, first of all the documents we presented before you were not before that Trial Chamber. And secondly, if my learned colleague is happy to rely on the findings of the Kordic Trial Chamber, I'm happy to rely on the findings that say that Blaskic was involved and was responsible for Ahmici, and I'm happy to rely on the findings that say that the defensive orders issued by Blaskic were a smokescreen, and I'm happy to find that he was working in concert with Mr. Kordic throughout the whole time. Regarding his claims about the war diary in relation to the Vitez Brigade, he claims that there's nothing in the war diary about the Vitez Brigade in Ahmici. Well, it's hard to imagine that this Court would order a new trial on that issue on the basis of something that isn't there. More importantly, if you look at the war diary, and you look at the orders I presented earlier today to you, one of the orders is at 2.00 asking that Cerkez report back. If you look at the war diary, there is an entry at 1355 asking Cerkez to contact Blaskic. There's also an entry between two of the orders asking Cerkez, or Cerkez contacting Blaskic and reporting the situation on the field. In light of those orders, it's quite clear what he's reporting. The appellant refers to the MUP report. Now, quite frankly, I find this somewhat difficult to comprehend. The part that appellant's counsel specifically refers to is that there was a clandestine meeting at the home of Dario Kordic where the decision was made to kill those persons in Ahmici. Now, unless I'm mistaken - and I'm more than willing to be corrected on this - there is no independent evidence in the admitted documents of that. In fact, if you look at the MUP report, that passage comes from an interview by Defence counsel, Anto Nobilo. I find it astounding that they would rely on a Defence counsel interview a long time after the events who said what happened as the basis for claiming that in fact there was this meeting unless, of course, Mr. Nobilo wants to get in the witness box and explain that to us. Other than that, I think the MUP report is of limited value, to say the least. In his submissions related to what is the fairest way or the most efficient way to deal with this, he goes on and on about the trial and the length of the trial and the issues to be resolved if there is a new trial, and the fact that he's willing to make concessions and that certain witnesses don't need to be tried -- don't need to be brought, excuse me. The issue before you today, in my respectful submission, is what to do with the additional evidence. This Appeals Chamber has the authority to remit the matter back to a Trial Chamber if it decides that it's not in a position to deal with the additional evidence. It does not order a new trial. There's -- as I've stressed, the merging of the admissibility standard with the standard for a new trial, in my submission, would be an incorrect way to proceed. The Kupreskic judgement permits you the authority to remand it to a Trial Chamber for the specific issue and, with respect, I can't accept the submissions by my learned colleague when he indicates that paragraph 70 of the Kupreskic judgement stands for the proposition that you can send it back for a new trial. If you're at all uncertain of that, I'll just point out again that the passage reads, "But in the more likely case that the opposing party challenges the voracity of the additional evidence, the Appeals Chamber is faced with a choice, either it can test the evidence itself to determine voracity, or order the case to be remitted to a Trial Chamber to hear the new evidence." I don't think it's equivocal. At one point in time, my learned colleague indicates that in response to, I think, Judge Guney's question, relation to the lines of authority, he says when there's different lines of authorities, for example, to the Jokers. You cannot assume that because there's different lines of authority that the one eventually leads to Blaskic. He says you must look at all the facts. Well, I would respectfully agree. I think you should look at all the facts and that includes the facts that the Prosecution has presented to you and the facts which we would present on this issue and the testing of the evidence. This case is not about Ahmici, though there's been much to say about this. This case relates to conduct over 14 months, many counts, and many different geographical locations, and it's the Prosecution's submission that many of the counts are not affected by the new evidence. And the chart has been given to you if you wish submissions, of course, by counsel for the appellant and by the Prosecution; we'd be pleased to provide them. I've certainly been called argumentative before, but never has any paper that I've presented to a court been called that. But if it is an argumentative chart, we would certainly be willing to make arguments on what counts are not affected. Part of the basis for the argument of the appellant that the evidence affects all counts is that the evidence goes to his effective control over all the forces in the HVO. I just bring to your attention one count, the count relating to Grbavica, which is the destruction or plunder of property under Counts 11 to 13. Under Counts 11 to 13, one of the counts in the Vitez municipality in September of 1993 is a place called Grbavica. The Trial Chamber convicted the appellant for the attack on Grbavica for the following reasons: The forces he used to participate in the attack were selected by him personally. This is -- I'm taking this from the judgement, Your Honours. "He personally, himself, participated in the attack. The units that participated in the attack were directly subordinate to him as was testified by one of the witnesses, it was the Jokers and the military police. The head of the military police by September was not Mr. Ljubicic but was a hand-picked commander, hand-picked by Blaskic who testified at trial and who indicated he was operating directly under Blaskic." The Trial Chamber found that his direct involvement in the attacks themselves were criminal. There is no new evidence which has anything to do with this count. And with respect, if the Court is seriously considering the -- my learned colleague's submissions, I would submit that you should consider the submissions by the parties on this issue and look hard at the issue of whether or not everything is truly affected. The Defence has conceded that it gives great deference to the Trial Chamber's findings and that, of course, it doesn't dispute many of the factual findings as found. That may be the case, but if we proceed to the appeal proper, I'd ask him to tell me whether he's going to continue in that vein in light of the fact that the appellant has challenged every single factual finding in the judgement. They've even challenged whether or not the number of victims in Ahmici are correct. With respect, you can't have it both ways. The main issue, one of the main issues, which may concern the Court is the scope and breadth of the material and the ability to hear this issue. With respect, there's a difference between a new trial where all these witnesses will be brought, some will have to be tested again, and the limited issue before you which is: Do the documents and the two witnesses warrant overturning a judgement of this length and magnitude? The issue is whether or not on the basis of the complete evidence to allow you to make an informed decision this should result in a new trial. The way to be informed of this is by -- of course the Appeals Chamber has the authority to do it or to provide it to a Trial Chamber for the single issue of the new evidence. That, I respectfully submit, is much different than the new trial which is being considered. On the additional evidence hearing, what is tested is the veracity of the witnesses or anything that goes to the impact of their testimony on the judgement. That is a very narrow matter, and it's very specific and has been limited by this Chamber in both Kupreskic, Musema, and Kambanda. At the end of the day, the appellant seems to merge two submissions. One, that the alleged misconduct or the failure to receive the documents somehow warrants a new trial and that the untested evidence presented to you from one side only warrants a new trial. I think my submission is fairly clear on both of those. The misconduct issue has not been determined by this Court, and with respect, with the exception of the Croatian archives, the other two issues are not something that is before you or can be determined. With respect to the second issue, I've already made submissions and attempted to inform this Court of why it does not have the authority at this stage under its own law; and secondly, if it does, why it should be so careful to proceed on a one-sided basis of the evidence. Subject to any questions, those are the submissions on behalf of the Prosecution for the purposes of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Farrell. Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, President Pocar. I congratulate you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Simply to repeat that I wanted to start by congratulating both you and Mr. Hayman for your very professional argument today. Two questions to you. The first one, you will recall that Mr. Hayman mentioned today some 25.000 pages of additional material which needs to be disclosed. Could you enlighten us on that a little bit? What is the state of that? Is that figure more or less -- does it correspond to it? Then I will have another question. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution, pursuant to its ongoing disclosure obligations, is reviewing material that has come in. The material that has come in could potentially include 25.000 documents that could be relevant. Sure, some of the panel is fully conversant in the procedures adopted by the Prosecution, but the initial search is simply a general search where you put in names of individuals, names of places, and it just -- what it does is it permits the team that's searching to pull out all documents that could potentially have some relevance, but the relevancy criteria are so broad that it would be anything related to Central Bosnia. So that is just the first step to take from that large pool of evidence the evidence that could potentially be relevant. There's no basis for claiming that this is going to be disclosed. It's just -- was for the purposes of the Court to understand the steps that we were taking and how long it would be before we could actually determine whether any of it was Rule 68. So, yes, there are 25.000 pages that could potentially be relevant. At this stage, it's just part of the process and certainly doesn't support the inference that they will all be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So how does this -- where do we stand on proceeding with the case then?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Sorry. On that, the original report, status report provided to the Pre-Appeal Judge was that it would take -- it was about a month ago, was that it would take about three months to review this material and disclose it. In light of our other disclosure obligations in other cases that may be pushed off a bit, but that was the original time period, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question is this: You have stressed in your argument today the need for the admitted new evidence to be tested, and I would benefit from your clarification. What would testing involved in the case of such documents of evidence apart from considering any documents that you may tender in rebuttal?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. In relation to the documentary evidence, it would be -- yes, it would be one of two things. If there are any witnesses who have specific knowledge about those documents and who can testify to them; and secondly, any documents in rebuttal or documents which clarify. And then, of course, the argument would be simply whether or not one of the documents is consistent with the other, which in the Prosecution's system is something that makes no distinction between this Appeals Chamber and the Trial Chamber. Both can do it and both have done it, so it certainly doesn't require a new trial for practical purposes except for the length of time it will take, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, but in this connection, if you had to submit evidence in rebuttal to this Appeals Chamber, how much time would you require for that? Taking in account the 25.000 documents, of course, but apart from that, apart from this three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: On the issue of these, of course the 25.000 have to be disclosed and my learn colleague has the right to review them. These, I suspect it would take - I don't know - three to four weeks. I think that it would take a -- I'm not sure. A month, a month and a half to put it. It wouldn't take that long. The material's been collected for the purpose of this argument -- most of it anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Hunt, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I want to take you up on your reference to Kupreskic and the test that was ultimately applied in that case. I think it was -- I haven't got it in front of me, and I think it was no reasonable trier of fact could have acquitted in the light of this additional evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That was indeed the test which was applied, but you'll notice that the judgement suffered a slight sea-change along the way, because at a different part of the judgement it talked about a different test. It compared the "could" affect the verdict or the findings of fact for the admissibility against "would" have affected the findings. The second one, the "would," being the proper test for determining whether there should be a new trial or an acquittal or whatever. And I wouldn't like you to think that that test which was applied in Kupreskic is one of universal application. It was appropriate in that case. But it surely is one about sufficiently of evidence. And despite all searches that have been made so far, it hasn't been demonstrated that this is a matter which was the subject of any submissions by the parties before the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry, Your Honour, I didn't -- despite searches so far, I'm sorry, I didn't understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Nobody has discovered that the test that was ultimately applied was the subject of any of submissions by the parties before that Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I may be missing the point and I apologise, but if what you're indicating is that no one submitted that that was the test to be applied --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: -- I think that's probably correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And I don't want you to think that it's going to stay as some sort of ultimate universal test.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's a very extraordinary one to say the least of it. It would make any party seeking to produce additional evidence -- I'm sorry. Once they got it in, it would make it impossible for that party to proceed in most cases, and that surely is not just.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Well, if I may, Your Honour, this was litigated, this very issue. In fact, Mr. Clegg, counsel for Josipovic made that very argument that you're making now that it should not be a high standard, that it would not result in fairness to an accused who had to meet the high standard of a "would," which is the equivalent of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, it is not. That's the point. I'm sorry to interrupt, but that's the difference. To say it would have affected is not the same as saying that no reasonable trier of fact would have acquitted. That's putting it very much higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: If that's your submission, then let me respond --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's not my submission. It's my suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Sorry. I'll make submissions, Your Honour, obviously, and I'm happy to hear your suggestions. With respect, this issue was litigated, and the Court did hear -- excepting your suggestion, but the Court did hear this and did hear the distinctions between "would" and "could" and did hear the argument that it should be "would" but still decided to apply this test. And with respect, the reason they did - and this is my reading of the judgement - is that as indicated in the decision, it says that it is trying to reconcile the test not with national jurisdictions but what would be applicable under the rules and practice of this Tribunal. And it also tried to reconcile it with Article 25 of the Statute where they have to make a finding of an error of fact. So at the end of the day, yes, what the Appeals Chamber did was it did decide that this was the appropriate test because it considers the evidence itself. It looks at the evidence, it hears it, and it puts it in the pool with all the rest of the evidence. It's then generally in a position to look at all that evidence and make a determination of unreasonableness of the verdict based on all the evidence, that which was before the Court and that which was not and has been heard and has placed in that pool. The purpose of doing that is it results in a consistency in approach in this jurisprudence as to what the standard is under Article 25, which is an error of fact results in a miscarriage of justice. The error of fact in this jurisprudence is one of essentially reasonableness of the verdict on a change of this magnitude, and the Court attempts to actually reconcile those very difficult issues in relation to Article 25. The Court has held in Tadic and in Kupreskic that you have to reach a standard under Article 25 before you can send it back under Rule 117. It doesn't say it could or it would or it might and then you send it back under Rule 117, and that's what the Court was trying to reconcile here. And it did result in this test, albeit very high, but this is the test that has been enunciated by the Appeals Chamber. And if this is not the test, then of course this Court needs cogent reasons to change the test. And if the Court determines that this test needs to be changed and that the Court has to determine whether there are circumstances under which a new trial is warranted, with respect, it doesn't mean that the proceedings, the procedural law as established in Kupreskic, goes out the window as well, the procedural law being that it has to be tested before you can make the ultimate determination. The only reference to support your suggestion, Your Honour, that one could find in the Kupreskic judgement is when the Appeals Chamber, and it's in paragraph 69, when the Appeals Chamber considers the change from "could" to another standard. In paragraph 69 it says, "The Appeals Chamber considers this change from the earlier Tadic formulation as more as a matter of timing than substance." The "would probably" standard is still basically appropriate for a miscarriage of justice has occurred requiring a reversal which supports your suggestion. The Court then goes on, and after considering that, comes to the decision as to what the test is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Farrell, both Tadic and Kupreskic went ahead to say that the Appeals Chamber decided that it would retry the facts, in effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: In Musema, yes, and Kambanda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And you've conceded and said several times it could be sent back for a new trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry if I have not made myself clear, it cannot be sent back for a trial. Kupreskic says it can be sent back for a trial on new evidence, for a determination on that matter alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's taking Kupreskic far beyond what the expressed words say, surely. What they're saying is that if they are going to try it, then that has to be the situation, but there is nothing in Kupreskic which denies the power of the Appeals Chamber under Rule 117 to say that it would be more appropriate for there to be a complete new trial. Now, wait a minute before you go on and repeat what you've said, let's concede for the moment that testing and all the rest of it has to go on before a new trial is ordered by a fresh Trial Chamber. That what you are now saying - I don't think you will find it expressly in Kupreskic - is that the Appeals Chamber has no power ever to send it back for a new trial by reason of the fresh evidence so that you may find that every witness has to be recalled before the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: The structure of the -- I appreciate your comments, suggestions, Your Honour. The structure of the test in Kupreskic, in my respectful submission, has four stages: The first is the admissibility stage; the second is the testing of the evidence; the third is the factual finding stage by the Appeals Chamber, let's just take the simple example of the Appeals Chamber, and then the application of the test. The admissibility stage, the testing, and then the factual finding which is the third one. Now, in the simple cases, the Court can do those factual findings itself; Musema, the other cases, Kupreskic, though not a simple case but on this scenario, let's say the simple cases. It's only, in my submission, in those circumstances where that factual finding cannot be made after the testing of the evidence by the Appeals Chamber or a Chamber for which it's been remitted because of credibility conflict that you're then not in a position to apply the test, you're not in a position to reach the last of the four steps, and that's where you can order a new trial. But not, on this test, simply at the admissibility stage, clearly not. And it's -- anyway, you are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that it was, and I thought I'd made that very clear. What I'm saying is that there's nothing in Kupreskic which would prevent this Appeals Chamber ordering a complete new trial. Now you've told me that that's wrong. Whereabouts in the judgement does it say that expressly?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May we appeal to the speakers to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We're both being punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: My apologies. I accept your comment. My submission, which you're fully aware of, is when you consider that these very arguments were made, when you consider that this issue was before the Court, when you consider that they could have ordered a retrial on this matter, and when confronted with the credibility issue, they said they had two choices, test it or remit it for hearing on the new evidence. It's my submission that you may be able to make the argument that it doesn't specifically deny it, but it doesn't permit it on the admissibility stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Gunawardana.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: Do you concede that the 47 exhibits and the two witnesses that Defence is seeking to call the evidence of those documents and the witness are admissible?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Admissible? Well, we've argued the admissibility stage already and the Prosecution has lost on those, so we concede that they are admissible at the very low threshold in relation to Rule 115. I may be misunderstanding your question, I'm sorry, but for the 47 and the two, I think we're bound by the Court ruling and they are admissible for the purposes under Rule 115 on that limited basis, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: If that is so, is it safe to leave the verdict -- is it safe to leave the verdict unchallenged? On this evidence admitted, is it safe to leave the conviction unchallenged?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Absolutely. The Court in Kupreskic and Musema, Kambanda did not find that once the documents were admissible, that the findings were even challenged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: So by sending it back for retrial, it is the review of the verdict that is being looked into, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. I think that's, at this stage, not either permissible or appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNAWARDANA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, if there are no other questions, we can ask the -- I'll ask Mr. Hayman to take the floor for his reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will try and be brief. It's startling to hear the Prosecutor say that the Prosecution of the accused was not, in large part, about the Ahmici massacre because that's certainly that's not how the case was tried. The case was tried by the Prosecutor of which the Ahmici massacre was the centrepiece. Most of the victims were from Ahmici, we had dozens and dozens if not 50 victims from that area that testified. The bulk of the trial was about the events on the morning of April 16th, 1993, and I think it is in that context that the new evidence which surely could change the verdict on -- as to whether the accused ordered the Ahmici massacre, which was what he was convicted of, among other things, surely that -- a change in the verdict of that nature would appropriately call into question the balance of the verdict. It was the linchpin, it was the heart and soul, it was what the case, in essence, was about, and it's the basis of his 45-year sentence. He wasn't sentenced to 45 years for allowing someone to be forced to dig trenches in some other part of the region. He was sentenced because more than 100 civilians died in that village on the morning, a very serious, heinous crime was committed. And our position was he was wrongfully committed of that and we want a chance to correct that grievous error. My colleague asked: Where's the error? It is as if the appeals briefs have not been filed in this case. They've been filed. You have our briefs on the appeal. The errors that we believe occurred are in the brief. The Prosecution has responded. We have spent a long period of time on this appeal to date, and we are not in the early phases; hopefully we're in the final phases. My colleague, I don't think, understood me fully with respect to why we believe the trial below was unfair with respect to the BH army archive, the HVO archive, and then the Rule 68 material. The only Rule 68 violations that we are alleging and that we, by the way, talk about and allege -- state in our appellate brief are the documents that the Prosecution had such as the Kordic case materials. The point with respect to these other archives is the Trial Chamber subpoenaed BH for documents, the accused subpoenaed BH for documents; neither of those subpoenas were adequately complied with. The Prosecution subpoenaed Croatia for HVO records. We participated in those hearings. We were at those hearings. We were entitled to participate, watch, when the documents arrived, and we hoped that they would, the Prosecution would have had a Rule 68 obligation to share the helpful documents with us. We were entitled to rely on those aspects of the Tribunal Rules, and the fact is the BH authorities blocked those subpoenas, the Croatian authorities blocked the Prosecutor's subpoena, and we didn't even get the Kordic material. So if you put it all together and that, that is why the trial below, not only was unfair, but it was unreliable. It's an unreliable process to have a trial when all that critical documentation is missing. There was mention of the Vitezovi, and I need to burden you with, by calling your attention to one more document, which I intended to reference in my earlier comments but I failed to do so. One of the new evidence documents that Your Honours have admitted is number 96 to, I believe, our first Rule 115 motion and it goes to the issue of the Vitezovi and this Mr. Kraljevic. I won't belabour the point, but if you'll step into the mindset, if you will, of the Trial Chamber for a moment as reflected in the judgement and the mindset expressed here today by the Prosecution. That mindset is: Blaskic had effective control of all the forces including this Vitezovi unit with young, well-armed men, very aggressive, et cetera. Well, what about Exhibit 96? This is a new report dated May 7th, so it's less than three weeks after the Ahmici massacre. It's a message from Colonel Blaskic to the Main Staff in Mostar query the connection, ownership of a petrol station. And what Colonel Blaskic says in this message is the Vitezovi have taken over a gas station and they're selling gas for their own enrichment. Paragraph 5, "Since Vitezovi PPN commander, Darko Kraljevic, is directly subordinated to you, please help us resolve this issue which is becoming increasingly complicated." He couldn't get gasoline for the regular HVO troops. The Vitezovi are selling the community's gasoline for their own black market welfare, and Blaskic can't do anything about it because he cannot control in a de facto sense the Vitezovi. He has to petition the Main Staff which is outside of the enclave, hundreds of miles away in Mostar, to help diffuse this crisis over the gas station and the gas. That's what was really going on. That's why these documents are important because they give you a flavour, perhaps in a silly, mundane way, they give you a flavour of what was really going on at the time. Now, I do need to respond, and I'm almost done, with respect to Grbavica, because I remember the testimony concerning Grbavica well, and my learned colleague refers to Grbavica for the proposition that even accepting all the new evidence, the Grbavica conviction should still stand, it doesn't have to do with effective control. The attack on Grbavica was a lawful attack on a BH army military installation. That's in the judgement. The order to attack was lawful; General Blaskic, Colonel Blaskic's order. What happened was after the attack, there was burning and looting by indeterminate, as I recall, forces or elements and the question was: Did Colonel Blaskic have effective control over the looters or not? Is he criminally responsible for what happened after the military action was over? And I submit to you, this is a good example of how the entire body of evidence, new evidence included, which now bears on the relative chaos, the confusion, the multiple lines of authority, the inability of Colonel Blaskic to punish groups like the military police, groups like the Vitezovi, did that render him with some element of control, even in Grbavica in September of 1993, with some element of effective control that is less than that with respect to which or for which he could be assigned criminal responsibility for looters that entered Grbavica after the military action? I submit to you this question as well as the other counts that don't directly involve Ahmici need to be reassessed by a trier of fact. The new evidence doesn't just go to Ahmici. There's new evidence concerning Kiseljak and lack of effective control. There's lots of new evidence about Busovaca and the death squad that was operating there at the direction of Kordic and Sliskovic. There is new direct evidence concerning attacks on Stari Vitez by the Vitezovi, initiatives of their own making, as I recall the evidence from memory. So the new evidence permeates the different counts of the conviction and Grbavica is no exception. It would be inappropriate for this Court to say, well, it's true the landscape has changed, this new evidence is truly significant as we have deemed these 50 items, but we're able to cut this little piece out and say: Nothing's going to change that. Nothing would have changed the Trial Chamber's views of that. Can you say that with certainty, beyond a reasonable doubt? We do not believe that you can. If you don't send this case to a Trial Chamber for a new trial, what's going to happen now? What is life for all of us going to be like? It is not a pretty picture and this goes to the efficient and orderly administration of justice. You will have to review the rest of the 115 items, we will have to get the remaining 25.000 documents, file more Rule 115 motions with respect to whatever is exculpatory. We will have to file more 115 motions with respect to whatever is exculpatory in these closed session Lasva Valley cases which we just got access to in September. There will be a full round of briefing on this 115 motions. The Prosecutor wants to file additional appellate briefs based on what is admitted under Rule 115, and then all the witnesses that need to be heard and re-examined need to be recalled. Now, I ask you: Is that the efficient and orderly administration of justice or would it be more efficient now to say: We have heard enough. We have these authorities under Rule 117 and Article 25. It is time for a new trial. Put all this to rest. Direct the parties, direct the Trial Chamber to do it in an efficient streamlined way that doesn't impair anyone's rights, and we can be done with a new trial before all the steps that I outlined could possibly be accomplished. I would be happy to try and answer any questions you may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayman. Do you have any -- please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, at a stage, I think about this time last year, the appellant was dragged, struggling to and obliged to file his appellate briefs before the fresh evidence was disclosed, having been given a fair amount of leeway in the meantime. And it was made clear to you at the time that having seen the additional evidence, you would be entitled to add to your appellate brief. That's the same that was in Kordic, and it's the general policy of the Appeals Chamber to do it that way at this stage. Now, you were arguing earlier on this evening that there had been a mistrial, in somewhat general terms, based upon the absence of this material at the trial and the findings by the Trial Chamber that by reason of their absence at the trial, they drew a number of adverse inferences against your client. Has that found its way into your appellate's brief yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour. We expressly point out and I recall because I was outlining my arguments this morning. In our appeal brief, we state that the Trial Chamber inferred from the absence of orders and from the absence of the SIS report investigating Ahmici that there must be other illegal orders that the Court didn't have access to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I know those references, but have you actually footnoted it from the documents that have come in?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My learned colleague is nodding vigorously up and down, and I take that as an emphatic yes. Without looking, I can't tell you what's in the footnotes exactly or brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I must confess when I looked at it, I wasn't looking at it from this point of view. But my recollection is you raised the argument that it was unfair for the Trial Chamber to have done so, but what I wanted to know is whether you have actually incorporated in those the material which has now come in. I believe your co-counsel says yes. I believe we can accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I believe we have because we filed our appeal brief after we filed our third Rule 115 -- I'm sorry, after we filed our second Rule 115, we hadn't filed the third, but the second, and we had the report, the SIS report by the second so that should be in our brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Good. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: May I put you a question, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: That may be of interest although it may be minor. You made the point in your previous submission that if we do not -- if we do not order a new trial by a Trial Chamber, there will be a violation of the right of appeal of your client. Now, is that your point that when new evidence is brought before the Appeals Chamber, that involves a redetermine -- possible Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. redetermination of facts, there would always be a violation of the right to appeal if the Appeals Chambers proceeds, itself, to redetermine the fact or are you relying just on the quantity of the evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, that there is a tension between the right to appeal and the mechanics of Rule 115. And as you move -- and I think Rule 115 envisioned a situation where a somewhat discrete and limited body of new material becomes available. It doesn't say that, but I think that that can be inferred. And as you move away from that paradigm towards sea-change type - I hope that translates - of documents possibly requiring the recalling of many, many witnesses, including experts and so forth, you move away from a more limited Rule 115 hearing and closer to a retrial. And there is a point -- what we're saying is there is a point at which you have moved close enough to a retrial that for that proceeding to occur before the Appeals Chamber, you are -- you would be inappropriately denying the appellant the right to an appeal from that ultimate verdict or decision. And from what I have seen and from I am hearing, more documents, more witnesses, we are closer to a retrial than what was envisioned by Rule 115, whether it happens here or below, such that we think the right to appeal is implicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Borderline would be, according to you, just the quantity, test of quantity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think it is the quantity and it is the nature. Here, there is -- the 45-year sentence was for the Ahmici massacre. At least 40 of those 45 years. I believe that with all my heart and soul. So if the evidence goes clearly and squarely to that offence for which the accused was convicted, is it appropriate for him to have a redetermination on that and then never have a right of appeal? That's my concern, as well as just the quantity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: If there are no more questions, we can conclude our hearing. So the hearing is adjourned.
